eslon-observations-magnetisme-animal-178:
Charles d'Eslon was a Paris doctor and Mesmer's chief disciple. His Observations on animal magnetism appeared in 1780, while the doctrine still rose and before the commissions of 1784 struck it down. D'Eslon pleads the medical case for the magnetic fluid in careful, earnest prose.

He reports cures he witnessed and answers the doctors who scoffed. His standing as a faculty physician made his support hard to dismiss. The book is the key pro-mesmerism tract of the early fight. Readers can hear true belief argued by a trained man of science. It shows how reasonable the fluid seemed before the blindfold tests.
europmc-pmc10212980:
Wu and co-authors review the blood-brain barrier in a 2023 paper, covering its structure, regulation, and role in drug delivery. The barrier is a tight lining in brain blood vessels that keeps toxins and germs out of the brain. That protection also blocks most medicines, which is a central problem in treating brain disease.

The review describes how the barrier is built and how its gates open and close. It surveys tricks to carry drugs across, from tiny carriers to focused ultrasound. The paper maps a key obstacle in brain medicine and the main ways around it.
europmc-pmc10247380:
Depp and a large team report that failing myelin drives amyloid buildup in Alzheimer's disease models, in a 2023 study. Myelin is the fatty coating that insulates nerve fibers and speeds their signals. It frays with age as its maker cells falter, and age is the biggest risk factor for Alzheimer's, for reasons still unclear.

In mouse models, the team found that damaged myelin prompts the deposit of amyloid-beta, the protein that clumps in Alzheimer's brains. Healthy myelin held those deposits back. The work links brain aging in the wiring to the disease's hallmark plaques.
europmc-pmc10365580:
Liu, Wang, and Liu weighed the use of ChatGPT in daily medical care in 2023. ChatGPT is a chat tool that writes text in reply to prompts. Clinics have begun to test it for real tasks. The authors survey what the tool can do and where it may cause harm.

On the plus side, Liu reports help with lists of possible diagnoses for a case. The tool also drafts patient letters, scan reports, notes, and discharge forms. That work can save staff time and cut errors. The authors still call the tool a double-edged sword. They urge care with wrong answers and patient privacy. Future work may add live tracking and care at a distance.
europmc-pmc11049480:
Roshandel, Ghasemi-Kebria, and Malekzadeh review colorectal cancer patterns, risks, and prevention in this 2024 paper. Colorectal cancer grows in the large bowel. In 2020 it caused more than 1.9 million new cases and almost 0.9 million deaths worldwide. It ranks third among cancers for cases and second for deaths.

Rates differ sharply between countries, mainly due to differing risk habits, the authors say. Prevention works on two levels. Primary prevention avoids risks such as alcohol and raises protective habits such as physical activity. Secondary prevention is screening, which finds and removes early growths before they turn cancerous. The review presents the latest evidence on spread, causes, and control programs. Open disputes remain over which factors matter most and which programs work best in each population.
europmc-pmc11186780:
Jin, Li, Jeong, Castro-Martinez, and Zuker map a body-to-brain circuit that reins in inflammation in this 2024 study. The body-brain axis senses organ function, metabolism, and nutrition, and steers them in return. The team asked how this axis answers an immune insult at the body's edge. They tracked signals between the vagus nerve, which links organs to the brain, and the brain itself.

Pro-swelling and anti-swelling cytokines spoke to distinct vagal neuron groups, they found. Silencing the circuit genetically let inflammation run unregulated and out of control. Switching the circuit on instead suppressed the pro-inflammatory response while boosting the anti-inflammatory state. Single-cell gene reads plus functional imaging identified the circuit's parts. The authors say selective control of this circuit could treat disorders from autoimmunity to cytokine storm and shock.
europmc-pmc1140680:
Mair, Piper, and Partridge test whether calories explain why eating less extends life in fruit flies in this 2005 study. Dietary restriction extends lifespan in diverse organisms, including mammals. In rodents it is often called calorie restriction, on the theory that total calories, not specific nutrients, drive the effect. The team asked whether the same holds in Drosophila, the fruit fly.

Cutting either yeast or sugar in the diet reduced mortality and extended life, they found. The gain did not track how many calories the food held. Per calorie, yeast had a much greater effect than sugar. Total calories, they conclude, are not the key factor in this species. The result points to specific nutrients, above all the protein-rich yeast fraction, as the lever. It challenges the assumption that findings from rodents transfer unchanged to other species.
europmc-pmc11415080:
Wang and colleagues review neutrophil extracellular traps in health and disease in this 2024 paper. Neutrophils are frontline white blood cells. They can expel their own loosened DNA, studded with inflammatory proteins, as web-like traps that catch germs. Understanding of these traps in infection, immune regulation, and disease has grown fast in recent years.

Excess traps can block vessels, damage tissue, and prolong inflammation, the review warns. They are implicated in autoimmune disease, metabolic disorders, and cancer. Yet the traps can also help: aggregated traps degrade inflammatory signal proteins, damping the response. Some traps act as autoantigens, targets the immune system wrongly attacks. The authors map the molecules and pathways that control trap formation. They frame that map as the route to therapies that tune traps up or down.
europmc-pmc1226180:
Mager and colleagues tested saliva bacteria as a sign of oral cancer in 2005. The cancer type was oral squamous cell carcinoma. It grows in the lining of the mouth. Early detection still poses a hard problem.

Saliva samples came from 45 patients and 229 cancer-free controls. Counts were taken for 40 common mouth bacteria. Three species stood out with higher counts in patients. Their levels gave useful accuracy for flagging cancer. Mager suggests a spit test could aid screening one day. More work would be needed to confirm the signal. The three species were Capnocytophaga gingivalis, Prevotella melaninogenica, and Streptococcus mitis. They flagged 80 percent of cancer cases.
europmc-pmc1241380:
Zarn, Brüschweiler, and Schlatter examined azole fungicides and hormone making in 2003. Azoles fight fungi on farms and in human medicine. Some also treat breast tumors by lowering estrogen. All work by blocking enzymes that build steroid hormones.

Two blocked enzymes matter most for side effects. One builds sterols that guide germ cell development. The other, aromatase, balances male and female hormones. High azole doses harm fertility and development in several species. Tests confirm many azoles block both enzymes in dishes and animals. Their aim is often poor, hitting mammal enzymes too.
europmc-pmc1241580:
Guvenius and co-authors measured pollutant exposure before and after birth in 2003. Four chemical groups were tracked: flame retardants, PCBs, PCB breakdown products, and pentachlorophenol. Samples covered mother blood, cord blood, and breast milk. Median PCB levels ran about 60 times the flame retardant levels.

Flame retardant patterns differed between mother and cord blood, unlike PCBs. PCB breakdown products made up 53 percent of PCB levels in cord blood. Pentachlorophenol levels were highest in maternal blood at 2,830 picograms per gram. Guvenius shows each chemical crosses to the baby by its own pattern.
europmc-pmc1615880:
Family trees in biology carry more data than the tree alone can show. Chevenet and co-authors built TreeDyn in 2006 to attach that extra data to tree graphics. Taxon facts and gene functions usually sit outside the diagram, forcing tedious manual work.

TreeDyn handles many trees in many windows, with texts and symbols projected onto leaves and nodes from annotation files. Users can query labels, highlight matches, and export graphics in standard formats or save sessions. Scripts automate repeated tasks, and a command line mode builds trees online. Chevenet supplies field-specific packages for common research needs.
europmc-pmc1808080:
Dromer and the French Cryptococcosis Study Group ran CryptoA/D in 2007, a France-wide study of cryptococcosis from 1997 to 2001. The disease is a life-threatening fungal infection caused by Cryptococcus neoformans. Most prior guidance came from trials in HIV patients with brain infection, run before modern HIV therapy.

The prospective study enrolled 230 patients without trial selection bias. Of them, 77 percent were HIV-positive, and 72.5 percent carried fungal serotype A rather than serotype D. Men, HIV-positive patients, and those whose fungus was serotype A all had more severe disease. Failure to clear the fungus by week two was tied to wide initial spread and to high blood antigen levels. Missing the drug flucytosine in early therapy also predicted failure, with odds near four times higher.
europmc-pmc1939880:
Covington and Harmer solved in 2007 a 70-year-old puzzle about why plants answer a growth hormone differently by time of day. The hormone is auxin, which steers plant growth and development in space, much as the circadian clock steers plant life in time. Early researchers noted the time-varying sensitivity but could not explain it.

Genome-wide activity profiling showed many auxin-induced genes are also under clock control. A glowing reporter assay confirmed that the plant's own auxin signaling rises and falls with the clock. Added auxin barely nudged the clock itself, so control runs one way. Both gene responses and growth responses to applied auxin were gated by the clock, meaning the same dose works differently at different hours. Many plant traits may thus hide a circadian layer.
europmc-pmc1942080:
Towner, Leroy and co-authors reported in 2007 the first detection of Marburg virus in a wild bat. Marburg and Ebola viruses cause hemorrhagic fever outbreaks that kill 80 to 90 percent of human patients. Finding their natural animal reservoir is a central open problem, unsolved nearly 40 years after the family was discovered.

In Gabon, the team found Marburg virus RNA and matching antibodies in the Egyptian fruit bat, Rousettus aegyptiacus, a common species. These bats are the first non-primate animals found naturally infected with this virus. The find also extends Marburg's known map into a new part of Africa, meaning more regions face outbreak risk than assumed. It parallels a recent report naming three fruit bat species as likely Ebola reservoirs, strengthening the bat reservoir case.
europmc-pmc1951780:
Stecher, Hardt and co-authors showed in 2007 that Salmonella uses gut inflammation as a weapon against resident microbes. The dense gut community normally shields the host by beating incoming germs, a defense called colonization resistance. How gut germs break that shield was poorly known.

In a mouse colitis model, the response that Salmonella Typhimurium provokes reshaped the gut community and held back its growth. A weakened mutant that cannot trigger gut inflammation was beaten by the resident microbes. Supplying inflammation another way, by adding normal Salmonella at the same time, or using mice prone to bowel inflammation, rescued the mutant's edge. Inflammation was thus both needed and enough to beat colonization resistance. The finding flips the usual framing: here inflammation helps the pathogen, not just the host.
europmc-pmc2125080: A medical paper with experiments on cultivating the microorganism causing epidemic poliomyelitis. The polio germ, grown. This article preserves that virology. The historical record keeps it. Such papers rarely see the light of day. The text survives intact.
europmc-pmc2125180: A medical paper on the relation of the spleen to blood destruction. The spleen again. This article preserves that hematology. The library keeps the document safe. Writers of history may cite it later. The paper lasts as a quiet witness.
europmc-pmc2125280: A medical paper on liver function as influenced by anesthetics and narcotics. The drugged liver. This article preserves that pharmacology. Scholars prize such firsthand sources. The paper lived through the years. It waits for future eyes.
europmc-pmc2125880: A medical paper on toxicity of certain widely used antiseptics. The poisonous antiseptics. This article preserves that toxicology. Future scholars will discover it. Its place in history is secure. Such papers rarely see the light of day.
europmc-pmc2128380: A medical paper with investigations on the oxygen content of cutaneous blood. The skin's oxygen. This article preserves that physiology. Its place in history is secure. Such papers rarely see the light of day. The paper lasts as a quiet witness.
europmc-pmc2130980: A medical paper on experimental production and transmission of tar sarcomas in chickens. The tar cancers. This article preserves that oncology. The archive keeps the paper open to all. Its pages add to the record of the past.
europmc-pmc2131080: A medical paper on the immunizing antigen of the pneumococcus, purification. The vaccine part. This article preserves that immunology. Those who study the era will use it. The archive keeps the paper open to all.
europmc-pmc2131180: A medical paper on the effect of mechanical tension upon the polarity of growing fibroblasts. The stretched cells. This article preserves that cell biology. It holds its historical place. Such papers rarely see the light of day.
europmc-pmc2131580: A medical paper on the relation of the liver to fat metabolism, effect of liver lack. The liverless fat. This article preserves that physiology. Its contents inform the historical record. The library keeps the document safe.
europmc-pmc2140880: A biology paper on stereotropism in rats and mice. The touch-guided rodents. This article preserves that animal behavior. Its pages add to the record of the past. Scholars prize such firsthand sources. The paper lived through the years.
europmc-pmc2140980: A biology paper on the geotropic reaction of rodless mice in light and darkness. The blind mice's gravity. This article preserves that animal behavior. The archive guards it with care. Those who study the era will use it.
europmc-pmc2361680:
Li, Uribe, and Daling compared the clinical features of nine breast cancer types in 2005. Breast cancer is grouped by histologic type, meaning how tumor cells look and arrange under a microscope. Rare types were poorly understood, so the team used a large US registry.

They analysed 135,157 invasive cases diagnosed from 1992 to 2001. Lobular cancers were more likely than ductal cancers to be large, advanced, and spread to lymph nodes at diagnosis. Inflammatory cancers showed the most aggressive profile of all. Mucinous, tubular, and papillary types looked the least aggressive. Hormone receptor patterns also split sharply by type. For example, 68.2% of medullary cancers lacked both estrogen and progesterone receptors, versus 19.3% of ductal cancers, a split pointing to different causes.
europmc-pmc2363380:
Senaratne and co-authors tested bone drugs directly on breast cancer cells in 2000. The drugs, bisphosphonates, are given to stop bone damage when breast cancer spreads to the skeleton. New patient data hinted they might also cut tumor burden in bone, so the team checked for a direct effect.

They exposed three human breast cancer cell lines to four bisphosphonates. All four drugs cut cell survival in all three lines. Zoledronate was strongest, halving growth at doses of 3 to 20 micromolar depending on the line. Pamidronate needed higher doses, and the other two were over a hundred times weaker. Treated cells showed the classic signs of apoptosis, programmed cell death: changed shape, broken DNA, and a cut marker protein called PARP. A protective protein, bcl-2, also fell.
europmc-pmc2568880:
Pruunsild, Kazantseva, Aid, Palm, and Timmusk dissected the human BDNF gene in this 2007 study. BDNF is a growth factor that supports neurons and shapes learning, memory, and pain, and its gene was known to be complicated. The team mapped the gene's full structure. They catalogued its alternative transcripts. They also tested where each version is switched on in adult tissues and brain regions.

They found 11 exons and nine working promoters, each used in specific tissues or brain areas. A partner gene on the opposite strand, called antiBDNF, produces noncoding RNAs with their own complex patterns. In the brain, BDNF and antiBDNF transcripts pair up into double strands. This suggests the antisense partner helps control how much BDNF is made in humans.
europmc-pmc2719080:
Ritchlin and co-authors issued treatment recommendations in 2009 for psoriatic arthritis for the Group for Research and Assessment of Psoriasis and Psoriatic Arthritis (GRAPPA). The disease mixes joint inflammation with skin and nail psoriasis, plus spine disease, swollen whole digits, and sore tendon insertions. Its forms and severity vary widely between patients.

Specialists and patients drafted nineteen recommendations from formal literature reviews for each disease form, covering peripheral joints, spine, skin, nails, and the digit and tendon problems. Members agreed on sixteen of the nineteen at over eighty percent. A grid that factors in severity for each form helps clinicians match treatment to the individual patient in front of them.
europmc-pmc2728480:
Ross and co-authors checked in 2009 how often clinical trials registered in ClinicalTrials.gov, the public United States trial registry, later appear in print. Selective publication distorts the evidence doctors rely on, since trials with dull or bad results often stay hidden. Registration was meant to create a public record that makes such hiding harder to sustain.

Looking at completed registered trials, they found low publication rates even after registration, with many trials still unpublished years after ending. Registration alone thus did not ensure that results reach clinicians, reviewers, or patients. The findings support stronger rules that require results, not just trial listings, to be posted and published in a timely way.
europmc-pmc2741580:
Hutton, Draganski, Ashburner, and Weiskopf compared in 2009 two MRI methods for measuring grey matter change in healthy aging: voxel-based cortical thickness and voxel-based morphometry. Both use standard brain scans, but one isolates cortical thickness while the other mixes thickness with surface area and folding. Regions with known age change were their test bed.

Overall the two methods agreed closely on where grey matter declines with age. The thickness method proved the more sensitive of the two, picking up age-linked decline more strongly. Since morphometry blends several anatomical features, using both together can separate true thinning from changes in area or folding. The pairing thus gives a fuller picture of how the aging cortex changes.
europmc-pmc2746580:
Aird and co-authors evaluated in 2002 thirteen novel ruthenium arene compounds as potential ovarian cancer drugs. Ruthenium is a metal, and these compounds may be less toxic than platinum drugs. Platinum drugs are active but suffer resistance and side effects. Ruthenium may act by a different route and keep activity where platinum fails.

Potency in the parent ovarian cancer cell line ranged widely. The best compound matched cisplatin, and two matched carboplatin. Certain ligand features raised activity, including a bidentate chelating group and a more water-averse arene. None of six active compounds was cross-resistant in the cisplatin-resistant line. One compound also worked in mouse tumors, including the resistant model, which merits further work.
europmc-pmc2817680:
Garrick, Taylor, and Fernando set out the correct math in 2009 for feeding breeding value estimates into genomic predictions for livestock. Breeders estimate each animal's genetic merit, its EBV, from records on the animal and its relatives. Those estimates arrive with uneven trust levels, and studies handled them in clashing ways.

The authors show that parent information must first be stripped out, then the estimate must be deregressed, meaning scaled back up by its reliability. They derive the proper weight for each record and prove that two common choices, using reliability itself or error variance as the weight, are both wrong. Mixed data, raw records on some animals and deregressed values on others, can then combine cleanly.
europmc-pmc2892080:
Sibal, Agarwal, Home, and Boger reviewed in 2010 the case against ADMA, a natural blood compound that throttles a vital vessel signal. Healthy vessel linings release nitric oxide to keep blood flow smooth, and low oxide marks failing linings long before heart disease shows. ADMA resembles the oxide's raw material closely enough to block its production, so high ADMA means impaired vessel function.

Levels run high in people with high cholesterol, high blood pressure, heart failure, diabetes, and kidney failure. In patients with coronary artery disease, ADMA predicted heart events and death more strongly than the traditional risk factors did. Early intervention work with the raw material L-arginine tries to outcompete the blocker, though the authors weigh its promise cautiously.
europmc-pmc2893180:
Leung and Wong reviewed in 2010 the pharmacology of ginsenosides, the active compounds behind ginseng's long medicinal reputation. These steroid-like plant molecules come in many variants that the body transforms step by step after swallowing, mainly through gut processing. The review first lays out their structures, how they change in the body, and how much actually reaches the blood.

From there it examines how ginsenosides interact with steroid hormone receptors. Those are the docking sites for cortisol and sex hormones. The contacts explain the wide spread of effects on inflammation, metabolism, and cell growth. That breadth makes them rich raw material for new therapies. One obstacle dominates, though: oral bioavailability is very low, so most of a dose never reaches its targets, and delivery science must fix that first.
europmc-pmc2920080:
Vandenberg and co-authors weighed in 2010 a puzzle about bisphenol A. The chemical is produced in huge volume for plastics and can linings. Blood studies find it everywhere, yet metabolism studies say it should vanish fast. Over eighty biomonitoring studies covering thousands of people in several countries overwhelmingly detected BPA in urine, blood, and tissues of adults and children.

The active, unprocessed form appeared routinely in blood at measurable levels. Two careful toxicokinetic studies, by contrast, predicted swift processing and excretion after oral doses, implying blood levels should be near zero. The review tests explanations for the clash, from non-food exposure routes and skin contact to slow release from body stores, and finds the discrepancy unresolved. Exposure science must settle it before health risk can be judged.
europmc-pmc2965880:
Cronin-Fenton and co-authors tracked hospital stays for blood clots in Danish cancer patients from 1997 to 2006 in a 2010 cohort study. Clots in veins often complicate cancer, yet which tumours carry the worst risk was poorly charted.

Nearly sixty thousand patients were compared with a general population group five times larger. Clot rates ran higher in patients overall and peaked in the first year after diagnosis. Pancreas, brain, and liver tumours, plus a bone marrow cancer, carried the highest rates, as did advanced stage and chemotherapy. Adjusted risks for some tumours rose many times above population levels.
europmc-pmc300680:
Lippman and colleagues dissected how jumping genes, transposons, are silenced and inherited in the weed Arabidopsis in a 2003 genetics study. Barbara McClintock first saw heritable yet reversible changes in transposon activity in maize half a century earlier.

Testing six transposons across mutant plants, they found most silencing lifted. The lift came when DNA methylation was lost. It also came when a chromatin remodeller or a histone editor was lost. Only a few transposons needed one histone methylator in particular. Others needed an RNA interference gene, or a second methylator. Crosses showed active states inherited unevenly by mutant type, and the patterns split the regulators into two interacting groups.
europmc-pmc3034180:
Hafner and coauthors linked in 2010 a longevity related enzyme to protection against age related heart thickening. As hearts age, a pore inside their energy producing mitochondria opens too often, weakening the cells. The enzyme, called SIRT3 in short, removes chemical tags from other proteins. The team found it strips one such tag from the pore's regulator protein.

Mice lacking the enzyme showed more pore opening and swollen mitochondria in heart cells as they aged. By just over a year old, their hearts were thickened and scarred, and they fared worse under added heart stress. A drug that blocks the pore regulator rescued the cell defect. The work points to the tag removal step as a guard against heart aging, and as a possible drug target.
europmc-pmc3052180:
Hoelzer, Moreno Switt, and Wiedmann reviewed in 2011 how people catch Salmonella infections directly from animals, rather than from food. Most cases of this illness are foodborne, but each year many come from contact at home, on farms, in zoos, and in vet clinics. Sick animals shed the germ more often, yet healthy looking animals can shed it for long periods too.

Risk depends on the animal species, its age and care, and on the person's own vulnerability, with young children and those with weak immunity at most risk. Some Salmonella types stick to one host species while others cross easily between hosts. Basic hygiene, such as hand washing after animal contact, cuts much of the risk. The authors note the public often does not know these risks, and they set out practical steps for homes, farms, and public animal displays.
europmc-pmc3106380:
Mohamed Daabiss published a 2011 review in the Indian Journal of Anaesthesia on a grading system used before surgery. The system, set up by a United States society of anaesthesia doctors, sorts patients into five classes by overall health, with an added mark for urgent cases. Daabiss asks how well doctors apply it in practice.

Studies show that grades often differ between doctors judging the same patient, even for common problems. Yet higher grades still track with more complications, longer stays, and higher death rates after many kinds of surgery. The review weighs calls to revise the scale and argues for clearer guidance, so a simple grade stays useful for planning, audits, and research.
europmc-pmc3117980:
Alex Becker and colleagues linked a hallmark Alzheimer protein to brain thinning in healthy older adults in a 2011 paper in Annals of Neurology. The protein builds up years before memory fails, and brain shrinkage follows a known pattern in the disease. The team asked whether build-up already tracks with thinning in people who still think normally.

Brain scans of nearly ninety healthy older adults and a smaller group with mild disease showed that higher protein build-up rose with age. In healthy adults it also matched thinner cortex in rear brain regions, in much the same pattern seen in mild disease. Shrinkage of a deep memory structure linked less steadily. The results suggest disease-like brain change begins well before symptoms.
europmc-pmc3129680:
Alessandro Varani and colleagues built a web pipeline for labelling jumping DNA in bacterial genomes in a 2011 paper in Genome Biology. These small mobile stretches copy themselves around genomes, reshaping them and spreading traits, yet genome reports routinely mislabel or skip them. Manual expert labelling cannot keep pace with sequencing.

Their pipeline combines prediction and labelling tools that follow the main expert database standards, handling one genome or many at once. It shows each element's setting in the genome and draws a map of their spread. Protein and DNA features are both recorded, which correct labelling requires. The authors offer the tool freely online, aiming to lift the quality of bacterial genome annotation overall.
europmc-pmc3149080:
Carol Bennett and colleagues found survey research lacks shared reporting rules in a 2010 paper in PLoS Medicine. Surveys underpin opinion, health, and policy research, yet sloppy reporting hides how a survey was run and blocks fair judgement of its results. Other research fields have adopted minimum reporting checklists; the team asked whether surveys had any.

They searched journal instructions and the published literature for guidance, reviewed evidence on survey reporting quality, and examined recent self-completed surveys against quality criteria. Guidance proved sparse and inconsistent, with no agreement on an optimal standard. Weak reporting of sampling, questions, and response handling was common. The authors lay the groundwork for developing a proper checklist so survey findings can be appraised and compared with confidence.
europmc-pmc3275480:
Jonathan Street and colleagues identified exosomes in human cerebrospinal fluid and profiled their protein cargo, in this 2012 paper in the Journal of Translational Medicine. Exosomes are tiny vesicles cells release, packed with proteins and RNA, already studied in several body fluids as a possible source of disease markers. Whether the fluid bathing the brain and spinal cord carries them had not been established.

Fluid from five surgical patients was concentrated by ultracentrifugation. Marker proteins, density behavior, and electron microscopy all confirmed genuine exosomes. Mass spectrometry detected a modest set of protein signals per person; about a third appeared in every participant, a third in only one, and quantities varied widely between people. The authors call the fluid's exosomes a promising new reservoir for neurological biomarkers, while warning that isolation methods need refinement to tame the variability.
europmc-pmc3280380:
Rebecca Dragovic and colleagues adapted nanoparticle tracking analysis to measure the tiny vesicles cells shed, in this 2011 paper in Nanomedicine. Microvesicles and exosomes carry messages between cells and promise diagnostic value, but measuring them was a bottleneck: electron microscopy is not quantitative and flow cytometry cannot see the smallest vesicles. The tracking method watches individual particles jiggle under a microscope and infers size from their motion.

Working with placental vesicles and human plasma, the team showed the method sizes vesicles down to about fifty nanometers, far below flow cytometry's floor, and counts them directly. Adding fluorescence, with antibody-tagged quantum dots stuck to chosen surface proteins, let them phenotype vesicles as well as size them. The authors offer the approach as a faster, more sensitive standard for a fast-growing field.
europmc-pmc3314680:
Partinen and a large Finnish team charted the same narcolepsy surge from the clinic side, reporting in 2012. Narcolepsy in young children was once very rare in Finland, with only a handful of cases expected each year. In early 2010, sleep clinics suddenly saw dozens of children struck by rapid onset sleepiness, prompting a nationwide count of cases from 2002 onward.

Fifty four children under seventeen were diagnosed in 2010 alone, a rate many times higher than the yearly average of the previous decade. Almost all had received the Pandemrix flu vaccine weeks to months before symptoms began, and all who were gene tested carried a known narcolepsy risk gene. Most also developed sudden muscle weakness, and emotional symptoms were common. Adult rates stayed flat, which the authors say points to the vaccine, likely with other triggers, acting on susceptible children.
europmc-pmc3380580:
Jjingo and colleagues tackled a puzzle in 2012 about DNA methylation, a chemical mark that usually silences genes when it sits at their start. Inside gene bodies the mark is even more common, yet there it tracks with higher activity. The team combined genome-wide data on methylation, gene activity, and chromosome state.

Genes carried more methylation than the stretches between them. The link with activity rose then fell: middling genes were the most methylated, while the quietest and busiest genes carried little. Blocking stray internal start sites explained only a small part of the pattern. The authors propose that access by the marking enzymes shapes most gene-body methylation instead.
europmc-pmc3428680:
Deng and co-authors built a math framework in 2012 for drawing ecological networks inside microbial communities from high-throughput data. Who interacts with whom in a microbe community matters for ecology, but extreme diversity and uncultured members make the structure hard to define. Their method borrows random matrix theory to set network links automatically.

The approach proved robust to noise, a chronic problem in sequencing data. Applied to soil communities under long-term warming, the networks under both warmed and control conditions showed the classic scale-free, small-world, modular shapes. Temperature and soil acidity emerged as key forces shaping the interactions. The whole pipeline was released openly online for other researchers to use.
europmc-pmc3467280:
Uematsu and colleagues charted how two deep brain regions grow from infancy into early adulthood, in a 2012 PLoS ONE study. The amygdala helps process emotion, and the hippocampus supports memory, yet few studies had measured them in babies. The team used MRI scans from more than one hundred healthy people aged one month to twenty-five years.

Both regions grew fast in the first years of life, then leveled off, reaching peak size around the start of the teens. Girls reached peak amygdala size about a year and a half before boys. Both sexes showed a larger hippocampus on the right side, while only males showed that tilt in the amygdala. Uematsu's maps give a healthy baseline for judging development in disorders.
europmc-pmc3493380: Brucellosis got a global burden review. This 2012 review estimates worldwide brucellosis cases. The authors reveal the frequency. Their work guides policy. Dean's team led the work. The paper is widely cited. It is a classic. It shaped livestock policy. The study shaped zoonosis policy.
europmc-pmc3532080: Sequencing reads got AdapterRemoval. This 2012 paper brings AdapterRemoval for cleaning dirty reads. The author reveals the tool. Their work spread through labs. Lindgreen's tool is open source. The paper is widely cited. Labs use it worldwide. It is a classic.
europmc-pmc3542080: Gut types got a body-wide guide. This 2013 paper maps gut-type communities across the human body. The authors map the communities. Their work guides microbiome research. Koren's team led the work. The paper is widely cited. It is a classic.
europmc-pmc3572580: ADHD got a causes review. This 2013 paper asks what we have learned about ADHD causes. The authors map the causes. Their review guides researchers. Thapar's review is widely cited. It is a classic. It shaped ADHD research. The review is widely taught.
europmc-pmc3591180: Liver cancer got an inflammation review. This 2013 paper reviews inflammation in liver cancer. The authors map the macrophages. Their review guides oncology. Capece's review is widely cited. It is a classic. It shaped liver-cancer therapy. The review is widely taught.
europmc-pmc3605280: MALAT1 got a cell-cycle role. This 2013 paper shows the MALAT1 RNA controls the cell cycle. The authors reveal the control. Their work guides oncology. Tripathi's team led the work. The paper is widely cited. It is a classic. It shaped cancer research.
europmc-pmc3626880: Psychiatry got a brain-inflammation review. This 2013 paper reviews brain inflammation in mental illness. The authors map the links. Their review guides research. Najjar's review is widely cited. It is a classic. It shaped depression research. The review is widely taught.
europmc-pmc3677880: Chromatin got diffReps. This 2013 paper introduces diffReps for chromatin-change detection. The authors reveal the tool. Their work spread through labs. Shen's team led the work. It is open source. The paper is widely cited. Labs use it worldwide. It is a classic.
europmc-pmc3860380: Alcohol got a stress-hormone review. This 2012 paper reviews stress hormones in alcohol dependence. The authors map the role. Their review guides psychiatry. Stephens's review is widely cited. It is a classic. It shaped addiction science. The review is widely taught.

frus-1861-d180:
Writing on 18 September 1861, William H. Seward sent a letter to Carl Schurz in Madrid. It is document 180 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

Enclosed papers gave an envoy proof and text to lay before a court. Schurz could use such matter in talks at Madrid the same week. The letter with its pack of papers shows diplomacy supplied like a brief for a case at law. Papers sent with a letter often held the texts of laws or notes for the envoy's use. A brief fit for a case at law is a fair image of the envoy's whole craft.
frus-1861-d280:
4 July 1861 is stamped on a letter Seward got from Mr. Haldeman. The printed record keeps it as Document 280 in the President's message volume for 1861. The date falls in the first summer of the Civil War, when the Union fought to keep foreign powers from backing the South.

The text is the view from the post abroad: local mood, official talk, and the envoy's own judgment. Its worth grows in context, as one link in a chain of letters that kept the peace with Europe. The State Department's Office of the Historian keeps the series, called Foreign Relations of the United States.
frus-1861-d80:
On 10 September 1861, Secretary of State William H. Seward wrote a second letter to Charles Francis Adams. It is document 80 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

The habit of paired letters served a clerical end: one point per paper. It also served a human one, since Adams could act on each at its own speed. The pair shows the Secretary's office at its most neat under wartime strain. The clerks who kept these files gave the record the clean order it still has. A clear order to the record serves readers a century and a half later.
frus-1862-d180:
Two Seward dispatches to London are dated 3 November 1862, and the first of them is Document 180 in the 1862 Foreign Relations volume. Both went to Charles Francis Adams, the American minister to Britain.

Early November brought the British cabinet to its choice on the French truce plan. London was close to saying no, which would leave France to act alone or drop the scheme. Seward's mail in these days armed Adams for the final round of talks. This letter is one strand of the pressure and patience that kept Britain neutral. The State Department printed the London mail in full for Congress, enclosures and all.
frus-1862-d280:
On 22 May 1862 William L. Dayton sent Secretary of State William H. Seward a report printed as Document 280 in the 1862 Foreign Relations volume. Dayton was the American minister in Paris, reporting on his post.

Late May found the war's focus on Richmond, where McClellan's advance had slowed to a siege pace. In Paris, the question of the hour was whether France would act with Britain on the American war or wait. Dayton's reports tracked that question through court and ministry talk. This one belongs to the quiet weeks before the summer's storms. A steamer's sailing day set the legation's week, and Dayton wrote against that clock.
frus-1862-d380:
Cassius Clay, the American minister in Russia, wrote to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 7 January 1862, opening the Russian file in the 1862 Foreign Relations volume as Document 380.

Russia was the great power most friendly to the Union in these years, and the St. Petersburg post carried a warmth the London and Paris files lack. Clay, a Kentucky abolitionist serving as envoy, reported from a court that wished the Union well. His early 1862 letters set the tone for the volume's calmest channel. Prince Gorchakov, Russia's foreign minister, made his government's sympathy for the Union plain. The Russian route was the longest in the file, crossing an ocean and then half of Europe.
frus-1862-d480:
On 16 September 1862 James E. Harvey wrote from Lisbon to Secretary of State William H. Seward. The report is Document 480 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, the year's official record.

Harvey wrote the day before Antietam, though no word of the battle could reach him for weeks. His subject was Portugal: its court's temper, its port rules, and its place in the Atlantic war of cruisers and blockaders. Reports written in such ignorance of home events have their own honesty; they show what a post knew and feared on its own evidence. Seward read them all before shaping his autumn answers to Europe. The letter keeps the Portuguese thread of that story intact.
frus-1862-d580:
On 7 September 1862 James Watson Webb sent this report from Rio de Janeiro to Secretary of State William H. Seward. It is Document 580 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, accompanying the annual message.

Webb wrote ten days before Antietam, in a hemisphere where the battle could not be known for many weeks. His subject was Brazil as he found it: its court's policy, its ports' practice, and the Union's standing there. Reports written in that isolation had to stand on the minister's own judgment, which in Webb's case was never in short supply. Seward read them for the southern facts of his global brief, and the September letter supplied them for the autumn file.
frus-1862-d680:
On 25 September 1862, Secretary of State William H. Seward wrote to a Mr. Blatchford. The letter is document 680 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1862, set between the China file and the Egypt papers. Unlike most letters in the volume, it was not sent to an envoy posted abroad.

Seward's desk work ranged far past the great powers. Letters to men outside the legations still formed part of the State Department's record, and this one was kept and printed with the rest. It gives a glimpse of the smaller business that crossed a secretary's desk in wartime, next to the fate of nations.
frus-1862-d80:
Dated 13 June 1862, a report from Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London went to Secretary of State William H. Seward. The printed record keeps it as Document 80 in the 1862 Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs volume. It belongs to the summer of 1862, the war's second year, when keeping Europe out of the war was a core task for Washington.

The text is the view from the post abroad: local mood, official talk, and the envoy's own judgment. For students of the war, the value lies in the sequence: one dated step in a long exchange. Foreign Relations of the United States, the official record series, is where the full exchange can be traced.
frus-1863p1-d180:
Reports like this one carried London news to Washington. This one went from Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London, to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 1 May 1863, and it is document 180 of the 1863 volume. The text is preserved in the 1863 Foreign Relations volume, which gathered the year's diplomatic mail for Congress and the public. It was one of 3 letters between the same men dated that day.

Mail crossed the Atlantic by steamship, taking roughly ten days or more each way. News in a dispatch like this one was already old when Seward read it, yet it guided his next orders. Kept with the rest of the 1863 papers, it forms part of the fullest record of how the Union handled its most dangerous foreign relationship.
frus-1863p1-d280:
On 4 September 1863, Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London, sent this dispatch from London to Secretary of State William H. Seward. It stands as document 280 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1863. The document comes from the Foreign Relations of the United States, the government's own published record of Civil War diplomacy.

Read in sequence, these reports show a diplomat testing how far he could push a stronger power without provoking a second war. That balance was the heart of Adams's whole mission. It belongs to the tense autumn when the fate of two Confederate ironclad rams in British yards hung in the balance. Set in its place in the volume, it helps readers trace how two governments talked their way past repeated crises.
frus-1863p1-d380:
Washington's business with Britain on 31 January 1863 included this note from Secretary of State William H. Seward to Lord Lyons, Britain's minister in Washington. The paper is document 380 of the 1863 volume. The letter is printed in Foreign Relations of the United States, the official series that publishes American diplomatic papers.

Britain had claimed neutral rights at sea, while the Union navy stopped British ships suspected of aiding the South. The friction from those seizures runs through this whole exchange. Kept with the rest of the 1863 papers, it forms part of the fullest record of how the Union handled its most dangerous foreign relationship.
frus-1863p1-d480:
W. Hunter, chief clerk of the State Department directed a letter to Lord Lyons, the British minister in Washington on 27 April 1863. At the time, the Union government was fighting the Confederacy at home and working to keep foreign powers neutral. It forms part of Foreign Relations of the United States, the official printed record of American diplomacy.

British subjects caught up in the war filled many pages: men arrested, goods seized, and claims for losses that London took up with Washington. The formal tone can hide the tension, but the pace gives it away. Notes this frequent mean both capitals were watching each other closely. The volume's editors printed it without comment; its meaning comes from the company it keeps in the file.
frus-1863p1-d580:
Document 580, dated 30 June 1863, records a letter from Britain's minister in Washington, Lord Lyons to William H. Seward, Secretary of State. Britain had not taken sides in the American war, and holding that line was the daily work of this mail. The letter was later printed in the 1863 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, issued with the President's annual message.

Read with its neighbors, the note helps explain a fact of the war: Britain never stepped in, and the record shows the effort that took. Trade ran through the whole exchange. British mills wanted Southern cotton, while Union officials watched every cargo for war goods bound to the South. It is a small, dated piece of a very large record, and it earns its place by keeping that record complete.
frus-1863p1-d680:
On 5 December 1863, Secretary of State William H. Seward sent fresh word to Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London. The dispatch is document 680 in Foreign Relations of the United States, the printed record of Civil War era talks with other nations.

December brought the close of a hard year. Gettysburg and Vicksburg had raised Union hopes, yet British choices still mattered a great deal. Seward's job was to keep Britain neutral and to guard American trade and rights at sea. This letter is one link in that chain. It lets readers watch policy move in real time, not in a later summary.
frus-1863p1-d80:
Charles Francis Adams closed a three-letter day with this dispatch of 13 February 1863 to Secretary of State William H. Seward. Adams was the American minister in London. The letter is document 80 in part one of the Foreign Relations volume for 1863.

The same date also drew a letter from Seward's side of the file, so the pens crossed that day on the Atlantic. Adams's third sheet rounds out his 13 February set. His winter mail kept a steady theme: Britain calm, the South's friends busy, the Union's cause held by care and facts. This letter is the last word of that day from London, filed with the rest.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d180: The Secret Protocol of the Moscow Conference, dated November 1, 1943, is Document 180 of the Cairo and Tehran volume. Protocols fixed in binding words what the ministers had agreed behind the public declarations, and this one was kept from print at the time. Its signing closed the first three-power foreign ministers' meeting of the war. The text, once secret, is printed in the Foreign Relations series, where readers can weigh what the allies promised each other in private.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d280:
The United States Chiefs of Staff issued paper C.C.S. 404 at Cairo on 22 November 1943, the proposed American agenda for the Sextant Conference. It is the detailed counterpart to the shorter British agenda printed next in the volume, and it lays out five heads of business.

After procedure and the overall objective, the European and Mediterranean head calls for enemy estimates, bomber offensive and anti-U-boat reports, the Azores facilities, and readiness reports on Overlord, Rankin, and Jupiter. The Japan head asks for a 1944 enemy estimate, a short-term plan for Japan's defeat, and reports on Southeast Asia, China, and the Pacific. A final head weighs resources against plans, asking whether the forces exist to carry out everything proposed.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d380: An editorial note in the Foreign Relations volume covers the Tehran dinner meeting of 1 December 1943, which lasted, by the President's Log, until half past ten at night. No official minutes of the conversation appear to have been prepared at the time. A memorandum written by Charles Bohlen a few days later indicates two things. The Declaration on Iran and the conference communiqué were discussed at the dinner. They were also put into final form there. The editors print this note in place of a contemporary record.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d480:
Secretary of State Cordell Hull wrote to President Roosevelt on December 4, 1943, the day the Second Cairo Conference opened. Hull remained in Washington while Roosevelt met Churchill at Cairo, fresh from Tehran. The cable appears in the State Department's published Cairo-Tehran conference volume.

Hull's cables were the department's way of sitting at a conference it had not attended in person. They brought Washington's news and views to the President at the moment decisions were being made abroad. For the reader, this message is part of the long-distance conversation that tied the traveling summit to the home government throughout December 1943.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d80: Churchill wrote to Roosevelt on October 31, 1943, and another Churchill note of the same date stands beside it in the volume. This one is Document 80 of the Cairo and Tehran volume. Halloween found the alliance counting Moscow's gains and drafting the November meetings. The catalog record gives the date and the two names and no subject. The message is part of the Foreign Relations series' dense autumn run.
frus-1944-quebec-d180:
An editors' note prints Harry Dexter White's memorandum of Roosevelt's talk with Morgenthau on September 13, 1944. White was not present; he summarized what the Treasury secretary told him. Roosevelt had summoned Morgenthau to Quebec to talk with Lord Cherwell, and over tea he went through the Treasury's book of memoranda on Germany item by item, setting limits on the discussion.

Morgenthau could discuss internationalizing the Ruhr and the Saar, including the Kiel Canal, Roosevelt said. He could even mention giving Holland a piece of western Germany for land the Germans had inundated. But occupation zones were a military question, and partitioning a political one; both were off limits. Eden was being sent for. "Don't worry about Churchill," the president added. "He is going to be tough too."
frus-1944-quebec-d280:
Amphibious craft, above all LSTs, are the subject of C.C.S. 687, proposed by the United States Chiefs on September 16, 1944. Accelerated operations in the Pacific and prospective plans for Southeast Asia required the earliest practicable withdrawal of landing craft from the European theater. The Combined Chiefs approved sending the message to Eisenhower, and it went out as Facs 81.

Eisenhower was asked to review the situation carefully with the object of an early release of craft from Overlord. Regard was to be had for his build-up needs until adequate port facilities became available, and for the weather limits on using such craft in the near future. An early report on the matter was desired.
frus-1944-quebec-d80:
Riddleberger wrote to Secretary of State Hull on September 4, 1944. He headed the Division of Central European Affairs at the department. His letter appears in the pre-conference papers of the Quebec 1944 volume. The conference in Canada opened eight days later.

A division chief reported upward as summit planning quickened. Central Europe faced occupation, new borders, and great human need. Hull needed his experts' judgment before advising the President. For readers, the letter shows the State Department's own chain at work. Regional specialists briefed their secretary while the Quebec agenda took shape.
frus-1945-50-intel-d180:
On 24 December 1946, the Chairman (Eddy) sent a memorandum to the Members of the Advisory Committee on Intelligence. It stands as document 180 in the intelligence volume of Foreign Relations of the United States, covering 1945 to 1950. The war had just ended, and the United States was keeping a central spy service in peace for the first time.

The memo form let a staff officer speak straight to a chief: here is the point, here are the facts, here is what is asked. The reply, if any came, would build on the points laid out here. Its worth lies in the trail it leaves: a dated, signed step in the long build-up of the CIA and the Council.
frus-1945-50-intel-d280: The title "Memorandum of Meeting" heads a text dated 28 May 1948. It is document 280 in the Foreign Relations of the United States volume on intelligence for 1945 to 1950. The CIA was in its first year, and the Council was taking up covert action for the first time. After key talks, an aide would write up what was said for the file.
frus-1945-50-intel-d380:
On 7 April 1949, staff wrote up the discussion at the 37th Meeting of the National Security Council for the President. In the printed Foreign Relations series it is document 380, in the volume on intelligence from 1945 to 1950. Reform talk filled the files that year, as the government weighed the Dulles team's harsh grades for the CIA.

A memcon lets later readers sit in on a talk they could not attend: who spoke, what was asked, what was left open. So the talk could guide later work, each point is set down while its weight is still clear. Alone it is a page; in sequence it is evidence of how a state taught itself a new trade.
frus-1945-50-intel-d80:
McCormack wrote to Under Secretary Acheson on 27 October 1945. The intelligence chief carried his office's case to the department's second-ranking man. Foreign Relations of the United States prints it in the later volume covering American intelligence between 1945 and 1950.

Acheson was the officer who most shaped the State Department's daily work, and his ear was worth more than most men's votes. McCormack's memorandum shows the intelligence office pleading its needs, staff, standing, or scope, at that level. Readers following the State thread should mark the Acheson papers: his support raised the office. His later doubts about its fit inside the department helped end its season at the center of American intelligence.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d180:
“Principal Yugoslav Problems” gives the bleakest reading of Tito's rise in the briefing book. Prepared on 27 January 1945 for the President's trip, the paper is printed in the Malta and Yalta volume. Its summary pulls no punches about who holds Yugoslavia.

The Partisan movement, it says, in fact controls the freed parts of the country. Its armed strength, the Soviet armies present under a formal deal with Tito, and months of British and Soviet support have built a powerful political machine. Rival groups, from Mihailovic's nationalists to the Croatian Peasant Party, sit in sullen impotence. All signs point to a firmly totalitarian regime to come. The Tito–Subasic agreement would hand real power to Tito's organization, with just enough exile faces to win foreign recognition.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d280:
Richard Law initialled the shipping agreement with a caveat, and explained it to Harry Hopkins on 14 January 1945. His letter, printed in the Malta and Yalta volume, concerns clause 10 of the American-British memorandum on supplies for freed Europe. Law was the British minister of state who signed for London.

Clause 10, as Law reads it, is a “no prejudice” clause. It leaves the present way of deciding shipping space exactly as it stands. Nothing in the paper settles, or even touches, what those procedures are or should be. He is sure it cannot fairly be read as changing them at all. Present practice, he notes, gives the military no veto over civilian shipping allotments. It does ensure the fullest exchange of information and consultation between the shipping authorities and the chiefs of staff.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d380:
Hold off. Secretary Stettinius's top secret cable to Ambassador Winant in London, sent February 7, 1945, orders a pause on France. In view of talks at Yalta, Winant was to take no action on the American position about France in German affairs. The cable repeats "no" for stress. He must wait for further instructions.

The freeze mattered because Winant had called a meeting of the European Advisory Commission for February 9. There he meant to announce American acceptance of France's request. Stettinius's wire stopped the announcement while the leaders settled France's zone and status. A copy went to Grew in Washington for his information.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d480:
A solemn warning to Germany is the subject of Grew's cable of February 6, 1945. The French Embassy had presented a formal note in Washington on February 3. France intended to warn the German government against maltreatment of, or reprisals against, French prisoners of war and deportees. Such acts would violate international law.

The French believed the warning would carry more weight, and might save thousands of lives, if issued by the United Nations as a whole. Paris sought clarification on one point: would the warning cover all United Nations nationals, not only French ones? Grew sent the matter on in case it rose at the conference. Left there, he would take it up in Washington.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d80:
Harriman was told to carry the President's words to Stalin in person. Secretary of State Stettinius sent the instruction on 5 December 1944, marked for the ambassador's urgent and personal attention. The cable, printed in the Malta and Yalta volume, opens the final push to settle Security Council voting.

Roosevelt's message says the Big Three meeting is still unsettled, so the voting question cannot wait. Agreement on it must come before a general United Nations conference can be called. Harriman is to discuss the matter with Stalin on the President's behalf, and the same approach is being made to Churchill. The cable then quotes the draft voting provision itself, beginning with one vote for each Council member.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d180:
Under Secretary Grew forwarded the revised British agenda to the President in a memorandum dated July 3, 1945. The short covering memo is document 180 in the Foreign Relations volume on the Potsdam Conference. It follows the trail of the original British list, sent May 30, and the Department's comments of June 14.

The British Embassy has now handed over a revised list of suggested topics, with comments, drawn up in a form fit to be shown to the Soviet government. Many problems on the first list have since been solved, as the Department expected. The new list runs mostly parallel to the Department's own draft agenda. The principal difference, Grew notes, is that it contains no topic on the Far East, an omission the Department pointed out to the embassy.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d280:
Ambassador Kirk reported a standstill over the British move into Styria in a telegram from Caserta on July 3, 1945. The message is document 280 in the Foreign Relations volume on the Potsdam Conference. Allied headquarters had directed the British Eighth Army to arrange with the local Soviet commander for a withdrawal from southern Austria.

On July 1 the British Fifth Corps commander met the Russians at Soviet Fourth Army headquarters and delivered the Eighth Army's letter. The Soviet commander said he had received no orders to withdraw and would hold his position until he did. A written reply the next day was cordial: the letter would go promptly to Marshal Koniev, but Soviet forces in Styria could not move without his orders. The episode mirrors the delays the Americans met over Berlin and Austria alike.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d380:
American and British reparations men met at Babelsberg on July 15, 1945, and a delegation memorandum records the session. Sir Walter Monckton led the British group; Pauley, Clayton, and others spoke for the United States. Clayton read the American paper's sections on war booty, labor services, restitution, and territorial cessions.

On war booty the British agreed in principle, but counseled against pressing the point. An agreed definition, they argued, would bind the West while not restricting the Russians. Pauley disagreed, saying the negotiations would drag on without end unless agreement was reached. The memo captures allied tactics, not just allied aims, on the eve of Potsdam.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d480:
British second thoughts on Allied Force Headquarters come in a memorandum by the British Chiefs of Staff representatives dated July 12, 1945. London has given further thought, it reports, to the dissolution of the headquarters and the organization that would follow it. The supreme commander, Mediterranean, and the commanders-in-chief, Middle East, have sent in their comments on the original proposals.

When those comments are considered, the British chiefs will put forward further draft proposals for the American chiefs. Meanwhile they agree to dispatching the message enclosed with the American paper, with one amendment. A substituted paragraph promises that the Combined Chiefs will send direction for the headquarters' future following the Terminal conference.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d580:
Japan's foreign minister, Shigenori Togo, wired his ambassador in Moscow, Naotake Sato, on July 11, 1945. The very secret cable, read here in translation, is document 580 in volume one of the Foreign Relations papers on Potsdam. U.S. officials held a copy within days of its sending.

Togo says Japan's state at home and abroad is very grave. Even ending the war, he admits, is now weighed in private. Tokyo's talks with Moscow aim not just at closer ties, but at sounding out Soviet help to end the war. He hints Japan could give up fishing rights won in 1905 to please the Soviets. He orders Sato to see Molotov at once and learn Soviet thinking. Yet Sato must not let Moscow sense that Japan hopes to use it to end the war.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d680:
A top secret briefing paper on the Montreux Convention was dated June 27, 1945. It is document 680 in volume one of the Foreign Relations papers on the Potsdam Conference. The 1936 pact set the rules for warships and trade ships passing the Turkish Straits.

The paper notes that Moscow aired its discontent at Yalta without stating its wishes. The Big Three agreed Russia would present them later for talks among foreign ministers. Washington has since told London it stands ready to discuss the Straits at the heads-of-government meeting. The paper remarks on an oddity in that stance. The United States never signed the Montreux Convention, yet Britain and Russia have drawn it fully into the question. Turkey, the state most affected, has not been consulted at all. U.S. interests are named as free commerce and a Straits regime that best promotes peace.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d80:
General John Deane, head of the U.S. military mission in Moscow, reported a Soviet refusal to Eisenhower on June 20, 1945. His urgent telegram is document 80 in the Foreign Relations papers on Potsdam. The Americans wanted General Parks's survey party admitted to Berlin at once; Soviet General Antonov would not move the date.

Antonov told Deane the question was being decided between the two governments, and he could not change his earlier decision to hold the survey until Zhukov returned around June 28 or 29. Deane notes that Harriman had raised the matter with the Foreign Office twice already, on June 15 and again the night before. They would keep trying. The exchange is an early taste of the slow Soviet bargaining style that marked the conference itself.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1080:
Foy Kohler, an assistant chief of Near Eastern affairs, recorded this conversation in Washington on July 25, 1945. The Greek ambassador had called to read a telegram from Athens. It quotes a Yugoslav note of July 23 demanding an end to terror against people of Yugoslav origin in Aegean Macedonia. Property was to be restored and reparations paid.

Athens calls the note a planned blow at Greek security and refuses to answer it. Greece has never recognized a Yugoslav minority, the telegram insists, and foreign meddling cannot be admitted. The refugees in Yugoslavia are branded collaborators or fugitive ELAS men. Greece will take no action, the ambassador adds, until it hears the American and British views.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1180:
The Secretary of State wrote to the President on 30 June 1945, more than two weeks before Potsdam opened. Papers from the run-up set the agenda and framed the choices Truman would face in Germany. The war in Europe had been over for less than two months.

Pre-summit messages did quiet, vital work. They sorted the questions, marked the hard ones, and lined up the facts the president would need. This letter belongs to that groundwork. It shows the peace being planned while the guns in Europe were barely cold. The summit's story starts here, not at the opening gavel.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1280:
General Deane, who commanded the United States Military Mission to the Soviet Union, wrote this memorandum on 24 July 1945. Deane's mission in Moscow was the American army's post inside the Soviet capital. He dealt with Soviet officers daily and knew their ways at first hand.

His memoranda carried that hard-won knowledge to the summit's staff. Few Americans had watched Soviet conduct as closely, or with as much friction, as Deane. A paper from his hand gave the team the Moscow mission's view. It is the soldier-envoy's voice in the record, blunt from experience.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1380:
W. Averell Brown, a special assistant to the secretary of state, wrote to both President Truman and Secretary Byrnes on 2 August 1945. That was the day the Potsdam Conference issued its closing papers. The text comes from the second Potsdam volume of Foreign Relations of the United States, the State Department's official history series.

A paper addressed to the president and the secretary together sits high in the pile. Brown wrote as the talks ended, when the results had to be summed up and carried home. Readers can place his memorandum at the hinge between the conference and what followed. First came the return to Washington and the reports to Congress and the press. Then came the hard work of making the Potsdam choices stick, in a world still at war with Japan.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d710a-80:
Benjamin Cohen's notes on the plenary session of July 23, 1945, compress the day's foreign ministers' report into a page. They are an unnumbered item in volume two of the Foreign Relations papers on Potsdam. Molotov read the report aloud, and Cohen tracked its points in order.

The economic subcommittee was told to study the Soviet reparations plans. On German economic principles, Russia withdrew her amendment to paragraph 13. She asked instead that paragraph 18 be deleted for further study by the Control Council, and no agreement was reached. The Council of Foreign Ministers proposal was approved with wording changes. On trusteeships, the Italian colonies' disposition was assigned to that council. Tangier produced a clean decision amid the disputes. It would return to its international status, with a four-power conference, France included, to meet in the near future.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d780:
Erhardt reported again on Austrian affairs on July 23, 1945, in document 780. The political adviser wrote to the Acting Secretary of State from his post among the occupiers. Austria's zones and its future government were live questions. His report joined the second Potsdam volume.

Follow-up reports show a problem refusing to sit still. Erhardt updated Washington as facts on the ground changed. Readers see occupation politics at working level: parties, officers, and rumors. The document adds ground truth to the summit's air. It reminds us that Potsdam's lines on maps had to be walked by men like Erhardt.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d880:
Willard Thorp, deputy to the Assistant Secretary of State for economic affairs, cabled William Clayton at Potsdam on July 25, 1945. Thorp reports a Washington meeting with British officials on German supply problems. The talks backed a zonal approach to buying and financing imports for occupied Germany.

Thorp quotes the British telegram that reported the American plan. Zone needs would be coordinated through CRAB, a joint supply body, using shared standards for food and industry. Shortfalls in one zone would be met from surpluses in others where possible. Import programs would go to the Combined Boards together, with equal priority for each zone.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d980:
Edwin Pauley and Isador Lubin sent this report on German reparations to the President on September 20, 1945. The printed text is an extract. It reviews their work from February to September 1945. Part V, shown here, covers the tripartite conference at Berlin, from July 16 to August 2.

Pauley reached Berlin from Moscow on July 14 with his senior staff. Talks with William Clayton's team shaped how to lay the reparations problem before the Big Three. The American proposals went into an annex on reparations. It held the seven agreed principles, the disputed first charge clause, and the agreed division of shares. It also offered definitions of restitution, war booty, and reparations.
gaius-institutes-muirhead-1880:
James Muirhead published his translation of The Institutes of Gaius in 1880. Gaius, a Roman law teacher, wrote the Institutes around 160 CE as a textbook for students. The text was lost for centuries and recovered in 1816 from a scraped parchment in Verona.

Gaius sorted all law under persons, things, and actions, a scheme that law teaching used for a thousand years. His plain style and clear order made Roman law learnable, and Justinian's own Institutes copied his plan. Muirhead, a Scottish professor of law, added notes for English students. The translation gives modern readers the Roman law school's own starting point, in the form that taught lawyers for a millennium.
gao-gaoreports-b-295780: AVL Books.Com shelved a March 2005 protest at GAO, and the ruling writes the last chapter. The bookseller's claims were read cover to cover. The story ended at the gavel. The final chapter closed. The gavel came down. The book was closed.
gao-gaoreports-b-297280: Alluviam took its December 2005 contract fight to GAO, and this ruling is the verdict on the claims. The firm said the agency's award was unfair, and the call tests the protest. Every challenger gets the full fair-play hearing. The process stays the same for all.
gao-gaoreports-b-299880: Kemron Environmental Services took its 2007 cleanup-contract fight to GAO, and this ruling is the verdict. gao-gaoreports-gao-06-580: Customs' trade computer was progressing in 2006, and GAO's report says progress had been made on the automated system, though long-standing issues remained. The findings balance credit and caution. The report warns that the border's digital gate needed finishing. The system had to work.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-780: The EPA's soot science was starting to move in 2006, and GAO's report says the agency had begun addressing the Academies' recommendations on health benefits. The findings track the start. The report warns that the particle math mattered for lungs. The work had to continue.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-80: Older workers needed better planning help in 2006, and GAO's report says Labor could help employers and employees plan for the future. The findings prescribe the aid. The report warns that the gray workforce deserved guidance. The planning had to be better.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-880: Medicare's hospital payment plan looked promising in 2006, and GAO's report says the proposed approach to inpatient payments appeared sound. The findings give the early nod. The report cautions that the new math still needed watching. The promise had to be proven.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-980: The Pentagon's travel booking system was a mess in 2006, and GAO's report says the claimed savings were doubtful and challenges remained. The findings doubt the math. The report warns that the troops' travel should not be a travel nightmare. The system had to work.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-280: Nursing-home asset games were rarer than feared in 2007 — GAO's report says few people shed assets before applying for long-term care. The findings calm the panic with data. The report's take: the loophole was much smaller than the outrage.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-380: The Army's future-combat dream had a fox in the henhouse in 2007 — GAO's report says the lead contractor's dual role raised oversight alarms. The findings question the referee-player setup. The report warns that the biggest weapons bet in history needed independent eyes.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-480: Guarding the sewers against terror had a price tag in 2007 — GAO's report totals the cost of vulnerability studies and risk plans for wastewater plants. The findings price the protection. The report's lesson: even the drains need defending in the age of fear.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-680: Profiling the jobless needed a manual in 2007 — GAO's report says the worker-sorting initiative wanted more guidance and a real evaluation of results. The findings question the sorting science behind the labels. The report asks whether the algorithm helped workers or just labeled them.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-780: The Pentagon could not say how hard it worked its people in 2007 — GAO's report finds the deployment-tempo data unreliable and the quality checks missing. The findings expose a blind spot on troop burnout. The report demands honest numbers on the human cost of the war rhythm.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-80: Phone competition needed better watching in 2007, and GAO's report says the FCC had to improve its monitoring of dedicated access markets. The findings target the blind spots. The report warns that the lines businesses rented needed a real referee. The market needed measuring.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-180: The Government Accountability Office dug into homeland Security: First Responders' Ability to Detect and Model Hazardous Releases in Urban Areas Is Significantly Limited in this 2008 report. Its findings feed into Congress's hearings and new laws. The library keeps it in the public record of federal watchdog work.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-280: GAO published its findings on information Security: Securities and Exchange Commission Needs to Continue to Improve Its Program in 2008. GAO digs into federal programs at Congress's request and reports back what it learns. Findings like these push agencies to fix the problems GAO reports.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-380: This 2008 report from the Government Accountability Office looks at no Child Left Behind Act: Education Actions Could Improve the Targeting of School Improvement Funds to Schools Most in Need of Assistance. Working for Congress, GAO checks how federal programs spend money and whether they deliver results. Its conclusions can shape how agencies run their programs.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-480: GAO published its findings on global HIV/AIDS: A More Country-Based Approach Could Improve Allocation of PEPFAR Funding in 2008. GAO digs into federal programs at Congress's request and reports back what it learns. Reports like this give Congress the facts behind funding and reform choices.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-680: This 2008 report from the Government Accountability Office looks at international Food Security: Insufficient Efforts by Host Governments and Donors Threaten Progress to Halve Hunger in Sub-Saharan Africa by 2015. Working for Congress, GAO checks how federal programs spend money and whether they deliver results. Findings like these push agencies to fix the problems GAO reports.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-80: The Government Accountability Office dug into economic Sanctions: Agencies Face Competing Priorities in Enforcing the US Embargo on Cuba in this 2007 report. Its findings feed into Congress's hearings and new laws. The library keeps it in the public record of federal watchdog work.
geheimnisse-einiger-philosophen-und-adep: Geheimnisse einiger Philosophen und Adepten, 1780. The philosophers' secrets. This book preserves that alchemy. The paper lived through the years. It waits for future eyes. It retains its place in time. The paper lived through the years.
grimm-teutonic-mythology-stallybrass-188:
Jacob Grimm, best known for the tales he gathered with his brother, built this vast study of German myth over many years. James Steven Stallybrass turned it into English in four parts from 1880 to 1888. Grimm worked from old poems, laws, and folk speech. He spent years in the work, and the notes grew to a vast heap.

The study traces gods, heroes, beasts, and rites across the old German world. Rune lore runs through it, tied to names, charms, and carved signs. Nearly all later work on German myth starts here, and its notes still guide those who study the north.
hering-guiding-symptoms-vol3-1880:
Hering's Guiding Symptoms reached its third volume in 1880, one more shelf of the ten-volume materia medica. The editorial team working from Constantine Hering's notes kept his system intact. Remedies appear in alphabetical order across the set, each with its full train of symptoms.

Mind, head, eyes, and the rest of the body each get their own sections within an entry. Odd and striking signs, the ones homeopaths call characteristic, stand out by their marks. Readers use the set as a court of appeal when smaller remedy books disagree, and Volume III does its share of that settling.
hering-guiding-symptoms-vol4-1880:
By its fourth volume, from 1880, Hering's Guiding Symptoms had settled into the shape prescribers relied on. Each remedy entry moves through the body in a fixed order, so a reader always knows where to look. Marks of differing weight point to the signs worth trusting most.

Constantine Hering died the year the volume appeared, leaving his notes to students who kept the work going.
