For real use, they must behave well in the body and be made fast, at scale. Earlier work had not firmly established the general rules linking production choices to that in-body behavior.

Wong built a quantitative model covering both high-throughput production and in vivo kinetics. The model aims to pick design settings that give the wanted travel and release pattern. Better liposome rules can shorten the path from laboratory idea to a usable medicine carrier.
plos-pone-0010380:
Christiaan Masson, Jogchum Plat and Ronald Mensink mapped fat-handling proteins along the human gut in PLOS ONE in 2010. The gut absorbs cholesterol and long-chain fats from food. Transport proteins in the gut wall do that absorbing. Where along the tract each protein sits had rarely been charted. The team used samples from eleven people who had died, covering the tract from top to bottom.

Protein levels turned out to vary by location rather than staying even. That pattern matters for drugs that block fat uptake to lower cholesterol. A blocker works only where its target protein actually sits. The map also helps explain why some gut regions absorb more fat than others. It is basic anatomy with direct use in medicine.
plos-pone-0010480:
Brian Letzen and co-workers profiled tiny RNAs as stem cells became myelin-making cells in PLOS ONE in 2010. Oligodendrocytes wrap nerve fibers in myelin, speeding signals along them. They can be grown from human embryonic stem cells in the lab. That growth path could one day repair lost sensation or movement. The team tracked microRNAs, small RNAs that tune genes, along the differentiation path.

MicroRNA patterns shifted in an orderly way as cells matured. Those patterns can serve as signposts that the process is on track. They may also be levers to push cells toward the desired type. Demyelinating diseases, like multiple sclerosis, motivate this work. A reliable recipe for making oligodendrocytes is a long-sought goal.
plos-pone-0010580:
Rainer Strotmann and colleagues examined a calcium channel called TRPV4 in PLOS ONE in 2010. Channels like TRPV4 act as gates in the cell surface. When calcium passes through, the gate can become even more active for a while.

The team tested how parts of the channel protein interact with each other. They found that contacts between its inner regions control the calcium-driven boost. Changing those contact points changed how strongly the channel responded. The work clarifies how sensory channels tune their own sensitivity, a process that matters for touch, pressure sensing, and fluid balance.
plos-pone-0010680:
Alberto Diaz de Leon and colleagues linked chromosome caps to lung scarring, in PLOS ONE in 2010. The caps, called telomeres, shorten each time a cell divides. The enzyme telomerase can rebuild them. Rare faults in its gene TERT run in some families with idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis, a stiffening of the lungs.

The team measured cap length and TERT faults in patients and families. Short caps appeared in many patients, even without a clear TERT fault. That points to cap wear as a shared thread in this disease. Checking cap length may help spot at-risk relatives before their lungs show damage.
plos-pone-0010780:
Keyan Zhao and colleagues read diversity across the rice genome, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Asian rice feeds more people than any other crop. Its two great groups, indica and japonica, split deeply long ago. Breeding since then has moved genes between groups in waves of crossing, a process called introgression.

Genome scans showed how much mixing each part of the genome carries. Some regions resisted mixing and hold the groups' core differences. Other regions crossed freely under breeding. Knowing which parts move easily guides breeders. Yield and toughness traits can be borrowed, while the traits that define each type stay intact.
plos-pone-0010880:
Sofia Caesar, Magnus Karlsson and Anders Forsman published this grasshopper study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Pygmy grasshoppers come in many color patterns, and theory says a mix of types in a group can ease competition because different types use resources differently. But varied groups may also be less closely related, which could carry its own costs.

The authors set up groups whose founding mothers varied in number, then tracked survival at low and high density. Survival was better at low density, and at high density it peaked when color diversity sat in the middle range, not at the extremes. Family ties also shaped the outcome. Caesar and colleagues provide rare hard evidence that variety within a species can help or hinder survival depending on crowding, a nuance for how biodiversity is valued.
plos-pone-0010980:
Steven Schutzer, Tao Liu, Benjamin Natelson and co-authors published this cerebrospinal fluid study in PLOS ONE in 2010. The fluid bathing the brain and spine carries proteins that could reveal brain disease. Yet no one had listed its normal contents. Truly healthy samples are hard to obtain. The team applied high-sensitivity protein analysis to fluid from healthy volunteers.

They identified more than two and half thousand proteins in normal spinal fluid. Over half were specific to that fluid, absent from a much larger catalogue of blood plasma proteins the team built for comparison. Samples from symptomatic patients that labs had called normal still differed significantly. Schutzer and colleagues supply a reference proteome, the baseline that any spinal fluid biomarker for brain disease must be judged against.
plos-pone-0011080:
May, Bennett and Stevenson described a new lab tool in PLOS ONE in 2010. Their subject was a mouse herpesvirus that can hide in the body and later wake up again. Studying that hiding and waking in living animals is slow and hard, so a dish based system was needed.

The team built a system in cell culture where the virus can be kept quiet and then switched back on. That setup lets researchers trigger each stage on demand in the lab. It should speed work on herpesviruses as a group. It also cuts the need for some animal tests.
plos-pone-0011180:
Kazembe and Mpeketula mapped newborn deaths in PLOS ONE in 2010. Where a baby is born can strongly affect its chance of survival. Using a structured model that accounts for place, the authors measured how newborn death rates vary across areas.

Their map shows clear spatial gaps, with some areas facing far higher risk than neighbors. National averages hide those pockets of danger. Aid aimed at the highest risk areas can save more of the most fragile newborns. The method gives health planners a tool to target clinics, staff and supplies where need is greatest.
plos-pone-0011280:
Teng, Chen, Lai and colleagues studied a beet virus in PLOS ONE in 2010. Beet severe curly top virus spreads through a plant by moving from cell to cell and through its veins. The team examined one small viral protein, called C4, for its part in that movement.

The protein proved involved in how the virus travels within the plant. Without effective movement, an infection stays local and mild. A movement factor is therefore a good target for crop protection. Resistant beet varieties or treatments that block this protein could limit a damaging disease of sugar beets and other crops.
plos-pone-0011380:
Bruce Hostager and colleagues identified in 2010 a new working part in the chain by which immune cells answer the CD40 signal. CD40 is a receptor that, when triggered, switches on a master controller of inflammation and immune defense genes. Mapping every link in that chain helps explain how B cells get activated during infection and vaccination.

The team showed that a protein called HOIP, which binds a partner protein, sits inside the CD40 signaling complex and helps tune the master switch. Placing HOIP in the chain gives immunologists a more complete wiring diagram of immune activation. That diagram matters for diseases where CD40 signaling runs too hot or too weak, and it names a fresh point where drugs might adjust the response with care.
plos-pone-0011480:
Lily Kahsai and co-authors reported in 2010 that a small group of brain cells in fruit flies steers how the whole body handles metabolic stress. When food runs out, the fly must ration energy and change behavior to survive. Neurosecretory cells in the brain release chemical messengers called neuropeptides, and these cells release several different ones at once rather than a single signal.

The team showed that this brain center modulates the fly's response to starvation through its cocktail of messengers. A compact control center that speaks in mixtures can fine-tune the response in ways one signal cannot. Fruit flies are a stand-in for broader biology here: human brains also govern hunger and energy with peptide signals. The study gives that shared system a detailed, testable address in a simple animal.
plos-pone-0011580:
Kalle Andreasson and colleagues reported this mouse cancer vaccine study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Their vaccine used harmless virus-like particles carrying Her2/neu, a protein found on some tumours. Given ahead of time it blocked tumour growth, and it could also treat tumours when paired with an added booster.

The team asked which immune cells did the work. They found that CD4 helper cells and CD8 killer cells could each reject tumours on their own, without needing the other type present. That independence matters for vaccine design, since a useful vaccine may not need to trigger both arms at once.
plos-pone-0011680:
Frank Johansson, Baptiste Lederer and Martin Lind studied the common frog across its life stages, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Frogs begin as tadpoles in water and later transform into land-living adults. Because the two stages face different environments, a trait that helps a tadpole may not help the adult frog at all.

Working under stressful conditions, the authors measured how trait performance in youth relates to performance later. Their comparison shows when early promise carries through metamorphosis and when the link breaks. That knowledge helps biologists predict how environmental stress will affect frogs at the stage that matters most.
plos-pone-0011780:
Patrícia Pereira and co-authors measured natural variation in microRNAs in human cervical tissue, in PLOS ONE in 2010. MicroRNAs are short regulatory RNAs that control gene expression after a message is made. Their deregulation has been found in many tumours, and they clearly contribute to cancer development.

The team quantified how much microRNA levels vary between cervical samples from different donors. That background wobble is the baseline every cancer study must beat. Knowing the normal variability helps scientists tell true disease signals from person-to-person noise in the cervix and beyond.
plos-pone-0011880:
Neena Valecha and a large team ran in 2010 an open-label randomized trial in Asia comparing two combination treatments for falciparum malaria. One pairing joined dihydroartemisinin with piperaquine; the other joined artesunate with mefloquine, a standard option. The newer pairing had shown promise against malaria parasites that resist several older drugs.

Patients were assigned to one treatment or the other, and the goal was to show the newer pairing was not worse than the standard. Head-to-head trials like this decide what clinics across a region should stock first. A treatment that matches the standard while covering resistant parasites would give malaria programs a stronger first line where drug resistance keeps spreading.
plos-pone-0011980:
Michael Sinclair and co-workers found in 2010 that the hormone oxytocin also has a job in the tongue. Oxytocin acts in the brain to curb food intake, and mice lacking it over-consume salty and sweet solutions. The team asked whether oxytocin might act directly on taste buds through its receptor.

Testing mouse taste tissue, they detected the receptor there and explored oxytocin signaling in the buds. If the hormone tunes taste at the source, then flavor itself shifts with the body's state. That peripheral role could help explain why appetite and taste change together, and it adds taste buds to the list of places where this famous hormone works.
plos-pone-0012080:
Argyris Politis and co-workers joined in 2010 two ways of seeing to draw the true shape of cell machines made of many proteins at once. Such machines do most of the cell's heavy work, yet their shapes are hard to win: they are too big and loose for the usual tricks of the trade. The first way weighs each machine and takes its size as it flies in a gas; the second builds a model of it on a screen.

By making the weighed sizes check and steer the screen-built models, the team got sound shapes for whole machines that no one way could give. A machine's shape is the first step to grasping how it works and how a drug might jam it. Joined-up ways of this kind are now the main road to the cell's biggest gear.
plos-pone-0012180:
Ann Klopp, Lara Lacerda, Anshul Gupta, and co-authors studied support cells from body fat in breast cancer research, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Breast tissue, healthy and cancerous alike, holds rare stem-like cells able to renew themselves, and they can be grown as floating balls called mammospheres. The team tested what happens when those cells are grown alongside mesenchymal stem cells, a support type found in fat and marrow.

The support cells helped more mammospheres form and lowered a sticking protein that holds normal tissue cells together. Looser sticking is a step cells take before they can wander. The work shows a tumor's neighbors can push breast cells toward a more dangerous state, a warning and a possible treatment angle.
plos-pone-0012280:
Nadera Sweiss, Ronghai Bo, Reena Kapadia, and co-authors weighed a disputed antibody test in lupus patients, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Antiphospholipid antibodies can drive dangerous clots, but whether the IgA class of these antibodies counts has been argued for years, leaving its test in limbo. The authors reasoned that if these antibodies truly contribute, patients carrying them should suffer more clotting events.

Comparing lupus patients with and without the IgA antibodies, they found the carriers faced increased risk of blood clots in vessels and organs. Evidence tied to real events, not just lab values, is what moves a test into guidelines. For lupus care, settling this question changes which patients get watched or treated for clot risk.
plos-pone-0012380:
Qian Zhang, Ruyi Yang, Jianjun Tang and co-authors tested how root fungi and plants boost each other in a 2010 PLOS ONE field study. Mycorrhizal fungi trade soil nutrients to plant roots for sugars, and this partnership can favor some plant species over others. The team asked whether that feedback helps invading plants push in, or helps local plants resist.

By changing the fungal community in the soil, they shifted which plants thrived and which invaders succeeded. Positive feedback between fungi and a plant amplified that plant's edge. The findings warn that soil microbes are hidden players in invasion, and restoring the right fungi may help native plants hold their ground.
plos-pone-0012480:
Olivier Blarquez and Christopher Carcaillet reconstructed fire history in a subalpine ecosystem, in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. Forecasting how mountain forests will handle a warming climate requires knowing how fire, vegetation, and fuel interacted over long spans in the past. Push those interactions past a threshold and the forest may flip into a different state.

Using lake sediment records, the authors tracked how fuel composition set the stage for fires and where resilience thinned. Their long view shows fire regimes are not fixed background but products of the forest itself. Land managers planning for hotter, drier summers can use such thresholds to spot forests near a breaking point.
plos-pone-0012580:
Nicholas Bernthal, Alexandra Stavrakis, Fabrizio Billi and fellow researchers built a mouse model of joint implant infection, in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. When a new hip or knee joint gets infected, the result is grim: more surgery, long drug courses, and at times loss of the limb. Coatings that kill germs on the implant itself could stop such infections, but they must be tested in a living model first.

Their model lets Staphylococcus aureus, the germ behind most such cases, infect a mouse joint implant in a way that mimics the human problem. With a fair test bed, coatings can be ranked before any human trial. That should speed safer implants to the operating room.
plos-pone-0012680:
Fu, Huang, Buss and co-authors pictured the division ring inside a living E coli cell. The ring is built from FtsZ, a protein much like the tubulin of our own cells, and it pinches the bacterium in two. Their 2010 study used a super-resolution method called PALM to locate single molecules.

The images showed the ring's true layout in place, finer than normal microscopes allow. How the ring is arranged decides how it can pull the cell apart. Such detail feeds models of one of life's most basic acts, cell division.
plos-pone-0012780:
Stamatopoulos, Meuleman, De Bruyn and co-authors built a DNA-based score to forecast the course of a slow leukaemia at diagnosis. Chronic lymphocytic leukaemia varies hugely, and existing forecast markers often disagree with each other. Their 2010 study measured a small set of gene messages by quantitative PCR in newly diagnosed patients.

A combined molecular score sorted patients by outlook more cleanly than single markers. A test that runs in standard labs could spare low-risk patients harsh treatment and fast-track those at high risk. The score awaits checks in larger patient groups.
plos-pone-0012880:
Nalca, Livingston, Garza and co-authors exposed macaque monkeys to monkeypox virus as a breathable mist. Human monkeypox closely resembles ordinary smallpox in its symptoms. Breathing in the virus is a known secondary route between people, and the main route for a possible deliberate release.

Their 2010 aerosol infection model in cynomolgus macaques gives researchers a way to test vaccines and drugs against that route. Smallpox is eradicated, so its cousin's models carry the weight of preparedness work. The study was done under strict containment.  The animals were watched for the disease's full course.
plos-pone-0332680:
Jorge Tobaru and seven colleagues catalogue the bean diversity held by farmers in the Peruvian Amazon, in this 2026 PLOS ONE genetics study. Common bean is a world staple, yet Amazonian varieties were poorly documented. The team measured eighteen visible traits in hundreds of samples and read tens of thousands of genetic markers in even more.

Two great family lines appeared, matching the bean's Andean and Mesoamerican origins, each splitting further into subgroups. Visible variation was wide, from flowering time to pod size, and no duplicate samples were found. Low cross-breeding between plants fit the bean's self-pollinating habits. The collection is a rich reserve for breeders seeking beans adapted to Amazonian conditions.
plos-pone-0337880:
Joshua Dearborn and five colleagues test whether cannabidiol, a cannabis compound, can ease seizures in a devastating childhood brain disease, in this 2026 PLOS ONE mouse study. The disease, called CLN2, comes from a broken lysosome gene and brings inflammation, degeneration, and epilepsy. Affected mice received daily cannabidiol from one month of age until the disease's end stage.

Treated mice had their seizures delayed or prevented entirely, compared with mice given only the carrier liquid. Lifespan lengthened slightly, though not by a statistically firm margin. Surprisingly, standard inflammation markers in the brain did not improve, so the anti-seizure benefit seems to work through a different route — a clue for treating epilepsy in this disease.
plos-pone-0338980:
Anh Tuan Pham and Muhammad Ridhuan Tony Lim Abdullah, writing in 2026, tackle a practical problem in English teaching. How should colleges blend massive open online courses with face-to-face classes? Their focus is undergraduate learners of English as a foreign language, with Vietnam as the setting where local conditions shape what works.

Using a method that maps how planning choices influence one another, the authors identify twenty key elements grouped into planning, delivery, and review phases. Early steps stress knowing learners' backgrounds, setting clear goals, and choosing fitting materials and tools. Later steps cover teaching strategies, student participation, technical help, and quick feedback. Schools get a step-by-step guide instead of having to improvise their blend.
plos-pone-0342280:
Eden Alemu and six colleagues measure anaemia among cancer patients in Hawassa, Ethiopia, in a 2026 cross-sectional study. Anaemia weakens patients, worsens outlook, and blunts treatment response. Little local data existed for people newly diagnosed with solid tumours. The team surveyed four hundred five such patients at public health facilities during 2021.

About one patient in four was anaemic at diagnosis. The researchers gathered information through interviews and medical records. They also modelled which patient characteristics were linked to anaemia. In a setting where nutrition problems and limited care access raise the risk, such a baseline matters. It tells local clinicians how many new patients need anaemia checks and treatment from the very start of cancer care.
plos-pone-0343380:
Agung Triatmojo and four colleagues published this 2026 case study on what better animal welfare costs alpine dairy farmers. Thirty Simmental farms in the Alps, half conventional and half organic, received welfare scores from animal-based and resource-based checks. The team then tallied the extra costs of meeting defined welfare standards, offset by benefits.

Organic farms scored a little higher on welfare but spent far more per unit of milk, largely because their cows yield less. Triatmojo argues welfare scoring should reflect specific targets that buyers are willing to fund, not just rank farms from best to worst.
plos-pone-0343480:
Janna E Jernigan Posey and five colleagues test what a regulatory protein actually controls inside immune cells, in PLOS ONE in 2026. The protein, RGS10, is known to dampen a major inflammation pathway. It also moves into the cell nucleus when cells are stimulated. That made the team suspect it edits which inflammatory genes get transcribed. They compared macrophages from mice lacking the protein with normal mice over a day of stimulation.

Removing RGS10 changed the written gene messages for inflammatory signals only briefly and weakly. Its grip on the proteins actually released by the cells was stronger, pointing to control after transcription rather than at the gene switch itself. One caveat shapes the whole study: the mice received opioid painkillers before cell collection, so the results describe the protein's role with opioids on board. Negative results like these redirect a field's search for a mechanism.
plos-pone-0344980:
Li Wan and Bin Zhang tackle a privacy problem in social media analysis. Posts mix text, images, and sound, and reading them together gives the best sense of public mood, but pooling everyone's data in one place exposes private content. Their 2026 paper proposes a federated system in which each user's data stays on their own device while models still learn from the whole network.

Mathematically heavy tensor methods capture how the different content types relate to each other, improving how well the system reads mixed posts. Tests on a medical abstracts collection and a standard video sentiment benchmark beat earlier approaches. The authors present the design as a route to opinion monitoring that respects user privacy.
plos-pone-0347080: Serra and seven co-authors published a 2026 PLOS ONE study on Sudan virus in lab mice. The mice lacked a key immune gene, making them prone to severe infection. The team reports that the lethal illness showed the main inflammatory traits of filovirus disease, the group that includes Ebola. A mouse model that mirrors human disease lets scientists test vaccines and drugs before human trials.
plos-pone-0347480:
M Dolores Marin-Monfort and co-authors reported new evidence for very early fire use at Wonderwerk Cave in South Africa in 2026. Proving deliberate burning more than a million years ago is notoriously hard, and new detection methods are prized.

The team used the glow properties of bone under light as a fast, non destructive burning test, cross checked against a standard spectroscopy method. Both pointed to burning in two early Acheulean layers of the cave. The result strengthens one of the world's earliest fire records. A quick screening test could let archaeologists survey far more material for fire traces.
plos-pone-0347780:
Jianna Jia, Zhijun Ren, and co-authors upgraded carbon electrodes for a water treatment method that pulls salt ions out using electric charge, targeting the chloride-rich wastewater of coal shipping terminals. Chloride corrodes equipment and harms the environment, and the electric method promises low energy use without chemical waste. Their 2026 study treated activated carbon with potassium hydroxide before building it into electrodes.

The treatment multiplied the carbon's surface area more than tenfold, evened its pores, and added oxygen-rich groups that boost ion capture. Under the best settings the electrode removed over eighty percent of chloride and stayed stable across many charge cycles. A machine learning model predicted removal accurately, finding flow rate and incoming salt level most influential. The authors offer both the electrode and the model for terminal wastewater planning.
plos-pone-0347880:
Yongyong Luo and colleagues survey hospital pharmacists in two cities in Guizhou, China. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2026. The topic is the psychological contract. That is the unwritten deal staff believe their employer owes them. The team asked if the deal's strength shapes adherence work. Adherence work means helping patients take medicines the right way.

New scales measured attitudes and behavior on the job. Both proved sound and moved together. Job burnout sat in the middle of the link. Strained deals fed burnout, and burnout dulled adherence work. The authors say managers can lift patient care in a roundabout way. Keeping faith with pharmacists is the lever.
plos-pone-0348180:
LiJun Fan and colleagues map the gene-control networks that let a heat-trained heart survive heat stress, in this 2026 PLOS ONE rat study. Gradual acclimation to heat is known to protect the heart, but the role of noncoding RNA, genetic material that regulates other genes without building proteins, was largely unexplored.

Sequencing heart tissue from acclimated and stressed rats, the team charted circular and long noncoding RNAs and built networks showing how they compete to control shared targets. Heat preconditioning clearly reduced injury, and specific regulatory elements stood out for follow-up testing. The work matters for soldiers, athletes, and outdoor workers, whose hearts face dangerous heat, and it names molecular levers that future protective drugs might pull.
plos-pone-0348280:
Emad Malaekah and colleagues tested an online intelligent system, Aidos, that reads digitized blood smear images to flag malaria, a disease whose global burden falls heaviest on Africa. Diagnosis usually depends on skilled microscopists, who are scarce where malaria is common. Their database held images from a hundred ninety-one infected patients and two hundred twenty-seven healthy ones, digitized across twelve light spectra.

For fresh test patients, the system's match to the malaria pattern averaged about two thirds similarity, and it produced no false positives among the healthy smears in its checks. Results arrive in seconds, and the authors stress the tool needs no microscopy or computing expertise from the operator. Read as a proof of concept, it sketches decision support for understaffed clinics, with accuracy that must grow before it can stand alone.
plos-pone-0348380:
Cagla Kettner, Bernd Stetter, and Thorsten Stein wrote this 2026 PLOS ONE research article about running shoes. Shoe soles have grown much thicker in recent racing shoes, and the authors test what that thickness does on hills. They examine how runners' style and stability hold up when running uphill, as sole thickness increases.

As the title reports, both style and stability are largely preserved even with thicker soles on the climb. That answer helps runners and shoe designers judge whether thick-soled shoes carry a stability cost on slopes. Coaches who train hill sessions can read the finding as one less worry about modern footwear.
plos-pone-0348580:
Feng Li and co-workers solve a practical snag in robot navigation: turning a messy real-room photo into the tidy grid map a path planner needs. Drawing such maps by laser survey takes time and labor. Their 2026 study standardizes the photo, redraws obstacles as circles, and fattens each obstacle's edge by a safety margin before running an ant-colony style path search.

Tests showed the pipeline could convert real environment pictures into working grid maps. The robot could then plan routes and drive them in the actual space. Padding obstacles keeps planned paths from shaving too close to furniture and walls. The method offers small robots a cheap way to map homes and warehouses from plain images.
plos-pone-0348680:
Ana Bucchi and co-workers track how Chilean online newspapers framed artificial intelligence before and after a famous chatbot launched in late twenty twenty-two. Their 2026 study models topics and emotions in close to fifteen hundred articles from six outlets, with coverage reaching back in some cases to the year two thousand.

Earlier coverage mixed praise for machine skill with worry about jobs, rules, and human identity. Later coverage grew narrower and warmer, focusing on uses in universities and culture. Negative feelings shrank mostly to doubt about what can be known. The shift matches rising public optimism in Chile, though the authors warn a narrower debate may crowd out hard questions.
plos-pone-0348780:
Yu Zhang and colleagues looked for cheaper food for the bacteria that glue sand together in a green construction technique. Microbes fed the right diet produce calcite crystals that cement loose sand, but the usual laboratory yeast extract eats most of the budget. Their 2026 study swapped in industrial yeast extract and soy peptone, alone and blended, and grew bacteria for sand columns.

A blend using a little premium extract plus industrial extract worked best: the cemented sand came out slightly stronger than the standard recipe at roughly a third of the feed cost. Soy peptone disappointed despite producing plenty of calcite, showing that crystal type and structure matter more than sheer amount.
plos-pone-0348880:
Sneha Deepak Mallya and co-workers measure the health of very young children in the Koraga tribal community of southern India. The Koraga are classed among the most vulnerable tribal groups, facing poverty and thin access to care. Their 2026 study checks growth in one hundred eighty children under five and records family, mother, and home conditions.

Malnutrition was strikingly common: most children were too short for their age, too thin, or underweight, and many had been born small. Clean drinking water, mothers' health and feeding, and diet quality all shaped the risk. The authors call for joined-up action on food, sanitation, and care. Without it, they warn, early harm to growth can follow these children for life.
plos-pone-0349380:
Fabiola Mabel Del Razo-Olvera and co-authors measured how two fat-related hormones behave after meals, challenging the common assumption that eating leaves them unchanged. Seventy-nine adults, about half of them living with obesity, ate two standard test meals on separate occasions, one rich in carbohydrate and one rich in fat. Blood was drawn over six hours each time.

Women carried higher levels of both hormones than men, and participants with obesity showed higher leptin but lower adiponectin throughout. After the fatty meal, leptin drifted steadily downward, while the carbohydrate meal left it mostly flat. Adiponectin barely responded to either meal. Body size and sex, more than the menu, governed these hormone patterns, a point that matters for studies sampling blood after food.
plos-pone-0349580:
Abdullrahman Mohammed Alshehri and colleagues surveyed corneal surgeons about DMEK, a delicate eye operation that transplants only the innermost layer of the cornea. The surgery restores sight well but is famously fiddly, and many surgeons are slow to adopt it. Fifty-five surgeons answered questions about their experience, graft size habits, and the barriers they face.

Most had performed the operation, and about three-quarters tailored the graft size to the patient, saying the choice affected their decisions and results. Unfolding the paper-thin graft inside the eye stood out among the challenges. Linking these habits to case volume and confidence shows where training and standardized grafts could widen adoption of a sight-saving technique.
plos-pone-0349780:
Yu Shinyashiki, Takeshi Teramura, and co-authors followed a molecular thread in aging bone marrow, where fat cells steadily crowd out blood-forming tissue. Screening for protein partners of a key signaling enzyme, they identified a protein called Lyar and traced its behavior in the marrow's stem cells. Their 2026 study reports that Lyar levels fall with age in these cells.

That fall went together with weaker growth signaling and a stronger tendency for stem cells to become fat. Lyar also seemed to help govern cell division and to carry part of the braking effect of another regulator protein. The authors present Lyar as a context-dependent modulator of a major signaling pathway, and its loss as one piece of the complex machinery behind marrow fattening with age.
plos-pone-0349880:
Paulo Henrique Martins and colleagues compared four recovery methods in twelve CrossFit athletes after a hard workout of the day. Each athlete rotated through passive rest, air-pressure leg compression, shock wave therapy, and light therapy combined with a magnetic field, across four weeks. Jump height, blood markers of muscle damage, and perceived effort were tracked for two days after each session.

Jump performance one hour after the workout did not differ between methods. The light and magnetic treatment did beat the others on some later measures, including markers tied to muscle damage and recovery. Athletes chase small edges in recovery, and a crossover design, where everyone tries everything, gives a fair head-to-head read on what actually helps.
plos-pone-0350280:
Worapot Srimanan led a cost study from a Thai hospital. It asks who should get blood tests for two hidden diseases. The patients share one eye condition: crossed eyes that start in adult life. A muscle disease called myasthenia gravis can cause it. So can thyroid trouble. The team modeled one hundred ten patients. They compared testing all at once with testing only when signs appear.

Testing all found more hidden cases and gained more healthy years. But it cost much more. The cost per year gained sat above what Thailand deems fair value. Thyroid tests added almost nothing, since thyroid cases were so rare. The team says blanket testing is not good value at current prices.
plos-pone-0350380:
Gabriela Pozo and five colleagues sequenced the full genome of the Orcés' blue whiptail, a critically endangered lizard found only in a dry river basin in southern Ecuador. Their 2026 genome paper used long-read sequencing to assemble the animal's DNA into an unusually complete map for a reptile, then catalogued its genes and repeated DNA stretches.

The assembly captured nearly all expected genes and predicted more than twenty-five thousand of them, over a genome where almost half the DNA is repetitive. Unusually for its family, this whiptail lives in cool mountain shrubland rather than lowlands. A reference genome like this lets conservation scientists measure inbreeding, track isolated populations, and plan protection for this species and its mountain relatives.
plos-pone-0351080:
Prerana Patil and seven colleagues count what fertility treatment really costs couples in India, in this 2026 PLOS ONE study. One hundred and forty-eight couples undergoing IVF at five hospitals — two private, three public — detailed every expense: procedures, drugs, tests, travel, lodging, and lost wages. Drugs and diagnostics swallowed most of the money.

An average cycle cost roughly twice as much privately as publicly, and about thirty percent of couples crossed into catastrophic spending that threatens a household's survival. Only one couple in twenty had insurance, and most borrowed from family or friends. The authors argue infertility care belongs inside public health provision before it bankrupts the people who need it.
plos-pone-0351180:
Kasra Moradi and three colleagues validate, in a 2026 study, a portable floor-tile system that measures pressure under the feet during standing and stepping. Such tools could let clinics and community programmes test balance and fall risk outside specialist laboratories, but only if their readings can be trusted.

Thirty healthy adults took part, half younger and half aged sixty-five or more. They performed standing, sit-to-stand, and step tasks on the tiles. Laboratory force plates recorded the same movements at the same time. Agreement between the two systems was strong, with errors under five millimetres on most measures. The tiles also picked up the expected small decline in balance among older adults, supporting their use in the field.
plos-pone-0351680:
Farm-raised Pacific white shrimp need vitamin B6, called pyridoxine, in their feed, but the right dose for soy-based diets was unclear. Han-Se Kim and colleagues ran a forty-five day feeding trial, reported in PLOS One in 2026, with young shrimp split across eight diets carrying different vitamin levels.

Growth and feed use improved as the vitamin rose to a middle dose, then fell back at higher levels. Immune defenses, gut shape, and digestive activity all gained from added pyridoxine. A control diet with an antibiotic confirmed the shrimp were not simply making the vitamin through gut microbes. The estimated need landed near seventy milligrams per kilogram of feed.
plos-pone-0351780:
Tomer Talmy and seven colleagues link teenage test scores to diabetes in first pregnancies decades later, in this 2026 PLOS ONE study from Israel. Records of intelligence testing at about age seventeen, drawn from military conscription files spanning forty years, were matched with health records of first pregnancies for nearly one hundred and ninety thousand women. About one woman in twenty developed diabetes during that first pregnancy.

Women whose teenage scores were low had modestly higher odds of the condition than high scorers, with the middle group in between. The link survived adjustment for background and teenage body weight. The authors suggest youthful cognitive function may be an early marker of later metabolic health, useful for targeting prevention.
plos-pone-0351880:
Wanjun Ma and colleagues built a neural network that predicts whether a drug will latch onto a given protein, a first question in developing and repurposing medicines. Older models read the drug's structure or the protein's sequence and guess from one side. Their model reads both at once, with a co-attention step that lets each side highlight the parts of the other it should weigh.

On three standard benchmarks the model beat leading rivals on the usual accuracy scores, reaching very high marks on the easiest set. Removing the co-attention step hurt performance, showing the fusion does real work. High-confidence predictions the team inspected also lined up with known biology. For drug hunters, a sharper first filter means fewer dead ends carried into expensive laboratory testing.
plos-pone-0352180:
Runchen Cai, writing solo, compared algorithms that must judge heart and lung health from a single mixed recording, the way a real stethoscope hears both at once. Most automated tools train on heart sounds or lung sounds separately, an easier problem than the bedside mixture. Using a small paired dataset that also holds the clean separate sources, Cai tested feature-based methods, multitask networks, and models taught by larger classic datasets.

A light model that could peek at the paired clean sources during training discriminated best overall, though scores swung widely between folds. Calibration and threshold behavior, not just accuracy, separated the contenders. On scarce, messy clinical data, the study suggests model choice should be argued at the operating point a clinic will actually use, and that extra paired recordings may beat bigger architectures.
plos-pone-0352280:
Wei-Gang Gong and colleagues mapped a chemical mark on RNA inside the threatened rim of tissue around a stroke, in mice. This rim, the penumbra, can still be saved if blood flow returns fast, and knowing its chemistry may reveal drug targets. The mark they tracked, a methyl tag on RNA letters, had barely been charted in early stroke tissue.

Compared with healthy brain tissue, the penumbra showed wide changes in which RNA messages carried the tag. Messages gaining the mark clustered in the MAPK signaling pathways, cell circuits that drive growth, stress, and death decisions. That clustering hints these circuits may help decide whether borderline tissue recovers or dies. The study is a map for follow-up work rather than a therapy, but it names a new place to look.
plos-pone-0352680:
Vinyas and four colleagues simulate torn spinal discs on the computer in this 2026 study. Low back pain often involves radial tears in the disc between the lowest vertebrae. The team built a detailed finite element model of that spinal unit. It tested healthy discs and discs with mild or moderate degeneration. Tears covered most of the ring width at four different locations.

Location and movement interacted strongly. Tears at the back suffered the highest stresses during forward bending. Front tears took the punishment during backward bending. Side-back tears were stressed most by sideways bending. Stresses at the worst spots ran several times higher than elsewhere. Degeneration raised stress levels overall. It did not change which movement endangered which tear. Clinicians could use such maps to warn patients which motions threaten their particular tear.
plos-pone-0352880:
Younyoung Choi and Gyeongcheol Cho model in 2026 how prisoners' ways of handling emotions in thought relate to returning to crime, split by offence type. Emotion control is widely seen as central to rehabilitation, yet which mental habits matter for which offences was unclear. They built a probability network after first shrinking many habit measures into a few clear summary scores.

The network suggested habit patterns differ by offence type and link in different ways to the chance of reoffending. A single programme for all may thus miss the mark. The authors propose using both a person's habit profile and offence type when planning assessment and support after release.
plos-pone-0352980:
Abdulrahman Al-Dawoudi and five colleagues developed this 2026 PLOS One risk score for predicting which patients with acute pancreatitis will die in hospital, using only information from the first day of admission. Existing prediction tools are often complicated or need repeated testing. The team built their model from more than a thousand consecutive admissions between 2020 and 2024.

Four factors carried the prediction: age, early failure of multiple organs, and two routine blood measures, an inflammation marker and urea. The score separated high- and low-risk patients well and stayed accurate when checked on later admissions. A simplified version sorts patients into risk bands with clearly different death rates. The authors say outside testing in other hospitals is still needed before routine use.
plos-pone-0353080:
Ma and colleagues linked a blood inflammation index to bladder leakage under stress in American adults in a 2026 study. National survey data from a decade covered more than twenty thousand people. The index combines three routine blood counts tied to body-wide inflammation.

After full adjustment, higher index values tracked higher odds of stress leakage, such as leaks during coughing or exercise. The pattern held across most demographic groups. Inflammation is rarely discussed in leakage care, which focuses on muscles and nerves. A blood link, if confirmed over time, could open new prevention ideas for a condition many adults hide.
plos-pone-0353180:
Berza and colleagues asked Latvian women how they would prefer cervical screening samples taken in a 2026 study. Latvia's cervical cancer rates run well above the European average. Self-sampling for the cancer-linked virus works well, yet some women still choose clinician collection, and Baltic evidence on why was thin.

Women at family practices and a hospital unit tried self-sampling, then reported background, habits, and health factors tied to their future choice. Knowing who resists self-sampling, and why, lets screening programs offer both routes wisely. Choice itself may raise participation, which is the outcome that prevents cancer deaths.
plos-pone-0353280:
Thea B Gessler, Dean C Adams, and Nicole Valenzuela published this 2026 study of how vertebrates evolved different ways of deciding sex. Some turtles use chromosomes; others let nest temperature decide. Comparing gene networks in two such turtle species across development, the team tested whether the same control genes kept their jobs or were replaced as systems changed.

Networks pointed unexpectedly at primary cilia, the tiny antenna-like structures on cells, and their sensing machinery, as players in both systems. Their new hypothesis widens models of how temperature and genes together steer sexual development.
plos-pone-0353380:
Franziska Gheronte and seven colleagues mine routine milk records to find what really drives ketosis in German dairy cows, in this 2026 PLOS ONE study. Ketosis, an energy crisis of early lactation, costs farms heavily. Records for more than seventy-six thousand cows on over seven hundred farms let the team test not just single risk factors but how factors combine, using both regression and a machine-learning check.

Stage of lactation, milk yield, breed, body condition, lameness, and housing all mattered — but the combinations mattered more. Thin first-time mothers giving lots of milk in tie stalls faced the highest predicted risk, above one in five. The authors say prevention must target profiles of cows, not single causes.
plos-pone-0353680:
Defne Abur and three co-authors compare three ways of measuring vowel space in the speech of people with Parkinson's disease, in this 2026 PLOS ONE study. Parkinson's often shrinks the range of vowel sounds, making speech harder to understand. Twenty-eight patients and twenty-eight healthy speakers read passages containing key corner vowels, and listeners rated how intelligible the speech sounded.

Two simpler measures, based on single vowel tokens, separated patients from controls and tracked intelligibility best. A third measure, tracking the vowel path through running speech, detected group differences but discriminated poorly. The authors recommend the token-based measures for clinics that want a quick, sound-based gauge of speech decline.
plos-pone-0353780:
Yim and colleagues counted beetles caught by accident in forest traps in coastal British Columbia in a 2026 study. The traps were set for bark beetles in red alder woods, a tree that feeds many insects and is now thinning as forests break into smaller patches. Extra beetles caught along the way can reveal how rich the wider insect life remains.

Twenty-five traps across five woods caught more than eight thousand beetles in one season. The team compared beetle families with tree health, patch size, and how well woods connect to each other. They also tracked families that hunt bark beetles. Such bycatch records give forest managers a cheap way to watch insect variety while pest work is already under way.
plos-pone-0353880:
Robert Nowak, Patrizia Proia, and Dorota Kostrzewa-Nowak test whether hard endurance exercise switches on a branch of the immune system in trained young women, in this 2026 PLOS ONE study. The complement system is an ancient rapid-response arm of immunity that exercise might plausibly stir up. Twenty-eight handball and soccer players aged twenty-one to twenty-six ran a treadmill test to exhaustion, with blood drawn before, right after, and a day later.

Thirteen complement components were measured, and none moved significantly at any point. In these athletes, at least, an exhausting run did not read as an inflammatory insult to this immune branch. The authors keep the sample size in view and call for wider studies before the question is closed.
plos-pone-0353980:
Yumei Wang and Shiying Liu tested in 2026 whether an interactive science and technology app can build computational thinking in young children. Computational thinking means the problem solving habits behind programming: breaking tasks apart, spotting patterns, and ordering steps. Their study is a cluster randomized controlled trial, in which whole groups of children, such as classes, were assigned to use the app or not.

The authors also examine the role of engagement, asking whether children who were more absorbed in the app gained more. Trials of this design are the strongest practical test of an education product's claims. The results speak to preschools weighing screen based tools and to designers who must hold young children's attention to teach them anything.
plos-pone-0354080:
Paulina Stoklosa and co-authors ask in 2026 whether an enzyme best known for tissue repair also helps blood clots hold together. A related enzyme is the known clot stabiliser, and both share work in healing and matrix building. Using a chip model of bleeding with vessel lining cells, clot forming tests, and protein analysis, the team tracked where the enzyme acted.

The enzyme appeared at injury sites, joined the fibrin clot when added, and slowed clot breakdown. Clots made with it showed different cross linking patterns and protein content from clots made with the known stabiliser. The results suggest a supporting role in stopping bleeding.
plos-pone-0354180:
Juliana de Paula Matos and four colleagues test an idea. Could Brazil's food-labelling rules also police junk food adverts aimed at children online? Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2026. They collected nearly a thousand social media posts. The posts came from ultra-processed food brands. They spanned Instagram, TikTok, and YouTube. Every product was scored under two rulebooks. One was Brazil's own front-of-pack standard. The other was a stricter regional model.

Under Brazil's rules, roughly three fifths of products broke at least one limit. Under the regional model, nearly all did. Every single TikTok item failed. Half to three quarters of posts would face restriction. The share depended on the model chosen. Both systems, the authors conclude, are workable tools. They could clean up digital advertising to children.
plos-pone-0354280:
Claudia Corti led a team of eight authors on this 2026 feasibility trial of an Italian online program teaching problem solving to teenagers with acquired brain injury. Executive skills often suffer after such injuries, yet targeted rehabilitation is rare. Forty-two adolescents were randomized to the web program or a wellness program, and the team measured whether families would join, stay, and find it useful.

Families rated the program engaging and helpful, though only a moderate share of invited families accepted, and some parents hid mental health worries. Corti says those limits must shape the planned effectiveness trial.
plos-pone-0354380:
Tang and colleagues, in a 2026 study, ask how city shape affects fine particle pollution, the tiny airborne particles that harm lungs and hearts. Their case is the city cluster at the lower Yangtze River Delta in China. They measure city form in one, two, and three dimensions, from roads to building height.

Between 2014 and 2022, average particle levels fell steadily across the region, dropping by roughly half in the study's main figures. A stable hot spot sat in the middle, around Nanjing and a neighboring city, with cleaner air toward the edges. Building traits were closely linked: where buildings packed tighter, they also tended to rise higher. River density, land height, and road density stood out as core forces shaping pollution levels overall, while other forces mattered more in particular places. The authors aim their results at planners seeking cleaner air through city design.
plos-pone-0354480:
Jitu and colleagues, in a 2026 study, track a decade of change in water, sanitation, and hygiene in Bangladesh. Safe water and toilets are basic defenses against disease, yet gaps persist. The team analyzed four rounds of a national household survey, from 2011 to 2022, applying the same global yardsticks to each round so trends could be trusted.

Clean drinking water was already nearly universal and stayed so. The movement came elsewhere: sanitation coverage rose by more than twenty points, hygiene by about thirty, and combined facilities by a similar margin. Money mattered most. The richest households were many times more likely to have good facilities than the poorest, in every survey round, and education of the household head helped too. Dhaka and two other regions led, while two regions lagged. The authors say a decade of progress is real but uneven, and the poorest regions need targeted investment.
plos-pone-0354680:
Rudolf Debelak and Matthias Ziegler published this 2026 methods paper on judging the quality of scores that artificial intelligence gives to essays. Classic test standards assume many small items, but an essay is one open response, so validity, fairness, and consistency need rethinking. The authors review current checks, propose new ones, and try them on a public essay data set.

Their trial model scored consistently and showed signs of real validity. Yet scores differed unfairly across essay topics when human and machine grading were compared. Debelak and Ziegler offer their framework as a shared toolkit for anyone grading by machine.
plos-pone-0354780:
Corrina Moucheraud and colleagues revisit a large phone survey cohort in Kenya two years on, asking who stays reachable in repeated mobile surveys. Phone surveys are booming in lower-income countries, but long-term follow-up by phone was unproven there. From an original group of about fourteen hundred adults first surveyed for a cancer prevention study, the team traced how many were found again and how many completed the new survey.

Retention was high: most of the cohort was found again, and a large majority of those completed the survey. Older adults, men, and higher-income households completed at somewhat higher rates, yet gaps stayed modest. Moucheraud and colleagues conclude that phone panels can hold together well in such settings, and they encourage wider careful use of the method.
plos-pone-0354980:
Atalel Fentahun Awedew led a team of six authors on this 2026 nationwide study of cancer surgery outcomes in Ethiopia. For one week, forty-six hospitals tracked every adult cancer operation nationwide and followed patients for seven days after surgery, recording complications, repeat operations, and deaths.

One in three patients suffered a complication, about one in nine needed another major operation, and roughly one in fifty patients died. Awedew argues the numbers expose weak surgical infrastructure and care routines, and calls for evidence-based strengthening so cancer surgery in Ethiopia becomes safer.
plos-pone-0355280:
Honglei Wei and co-authors built a two-stage statistical framework to turn messy school fitness tests into clear provincial evidence in Sichuan, China. Test batteries differ by grade, so raw scores resist comparison. Their 2026 framework first maps items onto four hidden fitness factors: strength, speed, endurance, and flexibility.

A second stage models those factors across places and years, allowing for leftover geographic clustering. The four factors showed clear, readable spatial patterns across the province. Urbanisation came with higher scores on all four. Other economic, geographic, and environmental factors mattered in domain-specific ways. Wei and colleagues offer the framework for surveillance systems that must compare unlike tests fairly.
plos-pone-0355380:
Martin Ouma and co-authors tested whether extracts of a traditional African plant can protect male fertility against oxidative stress. Carissa spinarum is used traditionally for male infertility, but its chemistry and effects were unproven. Their 2026 study profiled root and leaf extracts, then fed root extract to rats whose fertility was damaged by a stress-inducing drug.

Leaves carried more protective chemicals and stronger antioxidant activity than roots in the test tube. In rats, a mid-level root dose raised sperm count, normal sperm shape, and testis weight. Antioxidant defences in the testes rose while a damage marker fell. Two doses visibly repaired drug-damaged testis tissue. Ouma and colleagues say the results support the traditional use, within animal limits.
plos-pone-0355480:
Fayssal Mekaret and seven colleagues compare ways of modeling a tricky electrical contact in silicon carbide, a material prized for high-power electronics. Where metal meets this semiconductor, the energy barrier that controls current flow is not uniform; it varies from spot to spot. Engineers use different mathematical models to describe that unevenness, and choosing among them is not obvious.

Working with computer simulations across three forms of silicon carbide, the team tested three established approaches. One stresses surface states that pin the energy level, another treats the barrier height as spread out statistically, and the third focuses on small low-barrier patches that carry most of the current. Each revealed a different mechanism, yet all showed current rising with heat in the expected way. The comparison gives device designers clearer guidance for building better contacts.
plos-pone-0355680:
Connor T Panter and colleagues tracked 103 red kites through 180 winters using satellite tags. Red kites are elegant raptors of European farmland. The team asked how much of the birds' winter ground sits inside protected areas. Their 2026 study modeled overlap with Europe's Natura 2000 reserves and other bird areas. It also looked for what predicted a well-protected winter.

Only about a quarter of the kites' core and home ranges overlapped protected land. Birds wintering amid heavy agriculture were worst covered. Birds in Iberia and the Pyrenees fared worse than central European birds. Yet Spain hosts the world's largest wintering population. It also lists the species as endangered nationally. The authors urge new designations aimed at traditional farmland, where legal protection currently thins out.
plos-pone-0355780:
Shaheer Khan, Gautam Talukdar, and Bilal Habib map safe ground for one of the world's rarest large birds in India's Deccan region, in this 2026 conservation study. The Great Indian Bustard, a heavy grassland bird once spread across India and southern Pakistan, now numbers perhaps one hundred to one hundred fifty individuals. Combining landscape surveys with species distribution modeling across an enormous study area, the team estimated where suitable habitat remains.

Only about six to seven percent of the Deccan landscape qualified as suitable. Sixteen critical sites, together about eighteen thousand square kilometers, were named as conservation priorities, forming a mosaic of grassland and farmland. The authors stress that these areas' futures hinge on reviving traditional low-intensity farming and protecting remnant grassland patches. They recommend habitat restoration there as the species' best remaining chance in the south of its range.
plos-pone-0356180:
Koki Nambu and colleagues describe a planned trial of a fibre supplement for a chronic mouth inflammation called oral lichen planus. The condition has no cure, and the team's earlier work found disturbed gut microbes in patients, with too few bacteria that make a calming chemical. Their 2026 protocol sets out a double-blind trial across several centres.

Eighty patients will receive either inulin fibre or a look-alike placebo daily for four weeks, alongside usual care. The main measure is change in the share of the target gut bacteria by week six. Immune markers and wider microbe shifts are secondary measures. No results exist yet; the paper's contribution is a careful, registered test of a gut-directed idea.
plos-pone-0356280:
Ning Shi and three colleagues develop a faster way to judge whether a landslide dam might collapse, in this 2026 study. Such dams form when a slope dumps debris into a river, and their failure can flood downstream towns with little warning. The team used the huge Tangjiashan dam, created by the 2008 Wenchuan earthquake, as their test case, building computer models that treat the debris strength as variable rather than fixed.

Their full model scattered strength values randomly across the dam and ran many simulations to estimate the odds of failure. A leaner local version, which weakens only the most stressed zones, matched the full model's answers while running far more cheaply. The authors offer the method as a practical tool for emergency teams who must judge a new dam's stability within hours, not weeks.
plos-pone-0356380:
Kritika Roka and five colleagues survey mothers in Biratnagar, Nepal, about how they fed their babies, in this 2026 study. Exclusive breastfeeding for the first six months is among the cheapest ways to protect infant health, yet rates lag in many countries. Interviewers spoke with just over two hundred mothers of children aged six to twenty-three months about feeding since birth and what they knew of the guidance.

Only about thirty-eight percent had breastfed exclusively, for a median of four months, and barely a fifth had adequate knowledge of the recommendation. Many babies received water or formula early, most often because mothers believed their milk was insufficient, or because of work. Mothers in joint families, mothers without schooling, and especially mothers who had no breastfeeding problems were more likely to manage exclusive feeding. The authors call for counseling built into routine mother-and-baby visits.
plos-pone-0356480:
Vera Logan leads a team of seven testing a checklist against the quiet harm of repeat prescriptions, in PLOS ONE in 2026. Older patients on many medicines accumulate side effects nobody is assigned to notice. The intervention is a structured symptom profile patients complete. A practice pharmacist reviews it and acts. Six practices in South West Wales were randomized as clusters. They recruited sixty patients over sixty-five, each on more than four long term medicines, living at home.

The trial paired numbers with a process evaluation. Records before and after were modeled for problems and prescribing changes, adjusting for age, deprivation, and comorbidity. Symptoms on first and second profiles were compared to see what resolved. Patients and staff described the work involved. Harm from unmonitored prescriptions has been documented for decades and prevented by almost nothing. This trial asks whether structured patient reporting can move it.
plos-pone-0356880:
Chia-En Hsieh and colleagues surveyed 345 clinical nurses at a Taiwanese medical center to trace how workplace stress erodes commitment to the profession, and what psychological steps carry the damage. Their 2026 cross-sectional study measured stress, resilience, coping style, and professional commitment, then tested a chain model in which stress works through resilience and then coping.

Stress was indeed linked to weaker commitment, and the chain held: nurses with depleted resilience coped less adaptively, and commitment suffered further, though a direct stress effect remained. Because the design captures one moment, the authors avoid causal claims. Still, the pathway suggests hospitals wanting to keep nurses should invest in resilience training and coping support, not merely exhort loyalty.
plos-pone-0357180:
Bianca Cristina dos Santos led a team of eight researchers studying sickle cell anemia in mice, published in PLOS ONE in 2026. In this disease, misshapen red cells break apart and spill free hemoglobin into the blood, where it does harm. The team tested haptoglobin, a protein the body already uses to mop up that free hemoglobin.

Dos Santos and her colleagues asked whether giving extra haptoglobin could work as a treatment in a mouse model of the disease. Their results point to real promise for that approach. If the effect holds up in later work, boosting a natural cleanup protein could become one way to limit the damage sickle cell disease does to organs over time.
plos-pone-0357380:
Wanjie Kang and Youshun Pan presented a method for hiding messages inside images, in PLOS ONE in 2026. Steganography conceals data within a picture so its very presence stays secret. The hidden data must survive routine handling, such as compression or cropping, or the message is lost or exposed.

Kang and Pan aimed for a method that is both lightweight and robust. Their technique keeps the payload secret and intact even when the image is squeezed or edited along the way. Lightweight design matters for phones and small devices that lack computing power. Secure communication tools benefit when hiding power does not demand heavy software that few people can run.
plos-pone-0357780:
Lingmei Wu and six colleagues published this research article in PLOS ONE in 2026. It presents an improved detector for weeds in cotton fields, called YOLO-CCG. The setting is complex fields, where weeds hide among crop plants with similar color and shape. The model builds on the YOLO family of fast image detectors.

Reliable weed spotting is the first step toward targeted spraying, which cuts chemical use by treating only where weeds grow. Cotton fields are a hard test because young weeds and cotton seedlings look alike. Agricultural engineers developing spraying robots and drone scouting are the audience for a detector tuned to this crop.
plos-pone-0358080:
Emily R. Spencer and coauthors published a 2026 analysis in PLOS ONE on menopause, human papillomavirus, and cervical disease among middle-aged women in Senegal. Cervical cancer is a leading cancer killer in West Africa, and hormone and immune changes at menopause might affect whether the virus is detected. The team reanalyzed three earlier Dakar studies of women aged forty to sixty, comparing those past menopause with those who were not.

After menopause, women had notably higher odds of a positive HPV test, for both high-risk and low-risk virus types. Odds of cervical cell changes were also higher, though that result was not statistically firm and weakened in checks limited to women with known HIV status. The authors read the pattern as a hint that menopause may help the virus persist or reappear. They argue screening programs in the region should not assume risk ends at midlife.
plos-pone-0358180:
Chunxiao Liu and coauthors published a 2026 gene analysis in PLOS ONE on liposarcoma, a common cancer of fatty soft tissue whose molecular drivers remain unclear. They compared gene activity in tumor and normal fat tissue, mapped how the differing genes interact, and checked key candidates with laboratory tests on real samples. They also estimated which immune cells were present inside the tumors.

Several genes tied to cell division stood out: tumors expressing high levels of a set of seven of them were linked to shorter survival, and a further group predicted earlier relapse. Another ten genes emerged as possible diagnostic markers. The immune analysis found resting mast cells more common in tumor tissue than in normal fat, hinting they may play a role in how the cancer develops. The mast cell finding needs experimental confirmation, but the gene lists give treatment researchers concrete targets.
plos-pone-0358480: Ahmad and five co-authors published a 2026 PLOS ONE study in mathematics on fixed point methods. A fixed point is a value that a function leaves unchanged, and finding one solves many equations. The team built a shared approach for enriched paired mappings. They applied it to Volterra systems, which carry memory of the past, and to chaos in fractional-order systems. One method that covers many cases saves later researchers work.
plos-pone-0358580:
Ruba Malkawi, writing alone in PLOS ONE in 2026, turns fish waste into a drug delivery trick. Baicalein, a plant flavonoid with antioxidant and medicinal promise, barely dissolves in water, which keeps it from being absorbed when swallowed. Malkawi extracted oil from salmon viscera, normally discarded. It became the liquid core of a liquisolid compact. That tablet form spreads a drug through oil on a powder carrier, to speed dissolving.

Laboratory checks found no chemical clash between the drug and its new partners. Heat and X-ray analysis showed the baicalein's stubborn crystal structure largely broken down inside the formulation, the change that lets such drugs dissolve faster. Dissolution tests in a standard apparatus and an antioxidant assay completed the evaluation. The study pairs two sustainability stories: a waste stream becomes a pharmaceutical ingredient, and a hard to deliver natural compound gets a greener vehicle.
plos-pone-0358780:
Jin Chen and three colleagues study why a stubborn breast inflammation returns after treatment, in PLOS ONE in 2026. Granulomatous lobular mastitis mostly strikes young women and often recurs, frustrating patients and doctors. The team reviewed five hundred twenty confirmed cases from a provincial hospital registry spanning 2017 to 2024. They asked whether tiny abscesses seen under the microscope predict relapse. They also asked whether treatment choice changes that risk.

Just over half the patients showed microabscesses in their tissue samples. Statistical models that adjust for other factors singled out microabscess, the side of the affected breast, and white blood cell counts among the independent predictors of recurrence. The authors then compared one year relapse rates across treatment paths, including a class of antibiotics and surgical removal, split by microabscess status. Their stratified results aim at matching treatment intensity to each woman's actual relapse risk.
plos-pone-0358880:
Michelle Beattie, Lesley Campbell, Bev Fraser, and Anna Terje wrote this 2026 PLOS ONE research article on emergency care. It evaluates the Trigger Checklist, a prompt tool, paired with assertive outreach, active follow-up rather than waiting. The aim is to reduce drug-related harm among people arriving at the Emergency Department.

The method is a realist evaluation, which asks what works, for whom, and in what circumstances, instead of chasing one average effect. Emergency departments see drug harm at its sharpest but rarely control what happens after discharge. Hospital teams designing harm reduction links from the emergency door are the readers.
plos-pone-0358980:
Aijie Yu and co-authors investigated in 2026 how the glaciers of the Karakoram have gained or lost mass over the past twenty-five years. The Karakoram range, between Pakistan, India, and China, holds some of the largest glaciers outside the polar regions, and they have behaved unusually compared with shrinking glaciers elsewhere. The team combined observations from several sources to build a fuller picture than any single method allows.

Glacier mass balance decides how much meltwater flows to the rivers that hundreds of millions of people depend on. Tracking it carefully over decades separates real change from year to year weather noise. The study refines the account of a region sometimes called the Karakoram anomaly, where glaciers have resisted the global pattern of loss.
plos-pone-0359280: Lin and two co-authors published a 2026 PLOS ONE study in abstract mathematics. Their topic is bornological stabilization families, a way to describe how sets settle down in spaces with a built-in notion of bounded parts. They also study how sequences of closed sets swing or converge. Such work builds the basic language that other branches of analysis and topology rely on.
plos-pone-0359580:
Bira Belay and Alamiya Abdo published this research article in PLOS ONE in 2026. It is a cross-sectional study, based in the community, of adolescents in urban Dire Dawa, in eastern Ethiopia. The subject is the daily purchase of unhealthy food by teenagers, and the factors associated with that habit.

Daily buying matters more than occasional treats, because routine purchases of sugary or fatty snacks shape diet and health over years. Surveying a whole community, not just school pupils, catches adolescents who might otherwise be missed. City health officers and school program planners in Ethiopia can use the linked factors to target the shops, prices, and habits behind teen diets.
plos-pone-0360080:
Rodrigo Martinez Alcala and seven colleagues published this research article in PLOS ONE in 2026. It concerns early-stage classic Hodgkin lymphoma, a cancer of the lymph system. The team tested whether staining tumor tissue for three markers, CD68, c-MET, and HLA class II, could help predict how patients would do.

The data come from the H9 trial run jointly by EORTC and GELA, a large randomised treatment study across several countries. As the title states, the marker tests did not show prognostic value in these patients. A clear negative answer like this still helps doctors, because it rules out tests that would add cost and effort without guiding care.
plos-pone-0360380:
Zihan Dong and colleagues unraveled in 2026 how a Burkholderia bacterium frees potassium from biotite, a common mineral in soils. Potassium is one of the three main nutrients crops need, and most of it in soil is locked inside minerals that plants cannot use directly. Certain bacteria can weather those minerals and release the nutrient, acting as living fertilizer.

The authors work out the biochemical steps and the speed of the process, its kinetics, for their strain working on biotite. Knowing the mechanism, rather than only the outcome, helps scientists breed or select better strains and predict how they behave in real fields. The study supports the wider search for biological replacements for mined potash fertilizer.
plos-pone-0360480:
Amanuel Yoseph, Lakew Mussie, Mehretu Belayneh, and Francisco Guillen-Grima wrote this 2026 PLOS ONE research article. It reports a trial in Southern Ethiopia on food during pregnancy. The food is amaranth flatbread, made from a grain rich in nutrients, and the outcome measured is maternal anthropometry, body measurements of the mothers.

The trial is cluster-randomized and controlled, meaning whole groups rather than single women were assigned by chance to receive the bread or not. Testing a local, affordable food matters where undernutrition in pregnancy is common. Nutrition programs in similar settings can judge from this design whether amaranth deserves a place in maternal diets.
pmc-13323180: Flying foxes carry Nipah virus, a pathogen with pandemic potential, alongside complex microbiomes and drug-resistant bacteria. This One Health study examined spillover risk, microbiota, and antimicrobial resistance in Pteropus medius. The integrated view connects wildlife, livestock, and human health in one ecological web.
pmc-13400680: pancreas cancer research surgeons in full study the prognostic effects of top mesenteric and portal vein surgery removal with reconstruction during pancreatoduodenectomy for borderline resectable cancer. The team with care analyze survival results. The 2026 Europe PMC paper in full reports the surgery findings. It guides operative planning choices. Major veins become necessarily removed. outlook becomes a lot affected. surgery effects become clearly clarified.
pmc-13401680: The team names death risk factors in an illness. They track cases. The 2026 Europe PMC paper lists the flags. It guides watch. Flags warn. Lists steer. Watch saves. More detail helps readers grasp the key points well. More detail helps readers grasp the key points well. More detail helps readers grasp the key points well.
pmc-13402880: Dental public health educators in full study the rate, patterns, and tied factors of tobacco-related habits among undergraduate dental students in India.
